catalogTitle: Fulfilling the Destiny of כלל ישראל - to Return to their Roots - the אבות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yovel, Shavuos and the final Geulah all mean a return of Klal Yisrael to its roots, the level of the Avos, and that every Jew, even the lowest, carries a hidden point that will one day be brought back.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Ramban that the Geulah from Mitzrayim was complete only at Har Sinai, when the Jews returned to the level of the Avos, and calls this return Yovel. Shabbos and Shemitah are a return that one may refuse; Yom Kippur and Yovel pull everyone back. Following Rashi's question on Shemitah and Sinai, he links Yovel to the fiftieth day, Shavuos, and to the fiftieth level, which is hidden, as shown by the third-person 'hotzeisi osam' and the last word of Ana Bekoach, 'taalumos'. He then asks why the kedushah of Yosef and Serach protected all of Klal Yisrael but not Shlomis bas Divri, whose son the Arizal identifies with Yeshu. Her son needed the fiftieth level; yet even he has a good point, as the Gemara shows. The Mashgiach ties Yovel to hashavas aveidah, Rus's return, Rachel in Beis Lechem with a story, and the indelible point in every Jew.

en: According to the Ramban, the Geulah from Mitzrayim was completed at Har Sinai, when Klal Yisrael returned to the level of the Avos, and the final Geulah will restore that level fully.
Shabbos and Shemitah are a return that a person can decline, while Yom Kippur and Yovel bring everyone back, even against his will.
Shavuos, the fiftieth day, is Yovel and the fiftieth level, a level that is hidden and beyond the reach of the klalos and the sitra achra.
Every Jew, even the worst, has a hidden good point that never wanted to leave Hashem, and Yovel will bring it back to its root.
Yovel and Shemitah are a branch of the mitzvah of returning a lost object: everything lost goes back to its original owner.

title.en: The Geulah as a return to the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that the Geulah from Mitzrayim was completed at Sinai, when the Jews returned to the level of the Avos, and calls this return Yovel. He contrasts Shabbos and Shemitah, which one may refuse, with Yom Kippur and Yovel, which bring everyone back.

title.en: Shemitah, Sinai and the fiftieth level

summary.en: From Rashi's question why Shemitah is tied to Sinai, the Mashgiach links Yovel to Shavuos, the fiftieth day, and to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who finds the good point in every Jew. He brings the Zohar on the fifty mentions of yetzias Mitzrayim, the Ramak that the fiftieth is in this week's sedra, and explains why it is said in the third person.

title.en: Taalumos, and Shlomis bas Divri

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the last word of Ana Bekoach, 'taalumos', is the hidden fiftieth level revealed at the end of Sefirah, and mentions the Arizal's custom on haircuts. He then turns to Shlomis bas Divri, whose son the Arizal identifies with Yeshu, and to the kedushah of Yosef and Serach that protected Klal Yisrael in Mitzrayim.

title.en: Why the kedushah stopped short at Shlomis

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the kedushah of Yosef and Serach did not reach Shlomis, and answers that her son needed the fiftieth level, which they did not reach. He brings what he heard, that every Jew returns to his root after fifty thousand Yovlos, and shows from the Gemara about Onkelos and about Yehoshua ben Perachya that even Yeshu had good in him.

title.en: Yehuda and Dan in the Mishkan

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that the Mishkan was built by Betzalel of Yehuda, the foremost tribe, and Oholiav of Dan, the lowest, and that Nachshon ben Aminadav and Shlomis bas Divri are equal in gematria. In the hidden point even the biggest rasha is not a rasha, though it takes fifty thousand Yovlos to free it.

title.en: Yovel as hashavas aveidah; Rus returns

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Shemitah and Yovel a branch of the mitzvah of returning a lost object, brings the Baal HaTurim on the root 'geulah' in the sedra, and explains that Shavuos is the return of what was lost. He asks how Rus could 'return' to a land she had never been in, and connects Beis Lechem and Rachel Imeinu to the mitzvah of Yovel.

title.en: Rachel Imeinu at the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story he heard through Rav Mati Finkelman: a woman who was blessed with a child after davening at Kever Rachel invited Rachel to the bris, and an unknown woman of great beauty who appeared in every photograph came out blank in all of them.

title.en: The indelible point and every Jew's portion

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the shofar of Yovel and the point in every Jew that cries 'rotzeh ani', which remains even in those who have no share in Olam Haba, and brings Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's claim to exempt the world from judgment. He closes with every Jew's letter in the Torah and portion in Eretz Yisrael, and with Sefirah as earning by oneself what was given on Pesach.

catalogTitle: אדר סוף השנה' דורנו של עיקבתא דמשיחא סוף הדורות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the generations together form the body of Adam HaRishon, that our generation is its heel, numb and far from Yerushalayim, and that this is the hiddenness of Adar, the end of the year.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that all Jewish souls were contained in Adam HaRishon: Hashem kneaded the world like dough and separated Adam as its challah, which is why women bake and separate challah on erev Shabbos. Souls come from different limbs of Adam: from the head come those devoted to Torah, from the heart those devoted to tefilah, from the hands and feet those of chesed and mitzvos, and each person has his own shlichus. Every generation holds this whole structure, and so does the order of the generations: the head was the generation of Moshe Rabbeinu, the heart Dovid HaMelech, and we are the heel, the bottom of the foot, which feels almost nothing. This is ikvesa dimeshicha. In place too, Yerushalayim is head and heart, and the exile has pushed Jews ever further from it. Today even tzaddikim show nothing and Yiddishkeit is felt little; this is the hester within hester of Adar, which ends the year, and the joy of Purim is finding Hashem within that hiding.

en: Hashem kneaded the world like dough and separated Adam HaRishon as the challah of the world, on the first erev Shabbos; this is the root of separating challah on erev Shabbos.

Jewish souls come from different limbs of Adam HaRishon, and this sets each person's main avodah: Torah for those from the head, tefilah for those from the heart, chesed and mitzvos for those from the hands and feet.
The order of the generations is itself a full body of Adam: the generation of the desert is the head, Dovid HaMelech the heart, and our generation is the heel.

The heel is the least sensitive part of the body, and our generation has lost the sensitivity to Yiddishkeit that earlier generations had; the Mashgiach says our avodah is to be Jews even in this state.
In place as well, Yerushalayim is the head and heart of the world, and the exile has carried Jews ever further from it, to Bavel, Europe, America and the far west.
Adar, the end of the year, is hester panim, and today is hester within hester; the joy of Purim is that Hashem showed Himself in the midst of that hiding.

title.en: Adam HaRishon as the challah of the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara on the passuk in Iyov that all Jewish souls were in Adam HaRishon, and explains that Hashem kneaded the world like dough and separated Adam as its challah on the first erev Shabbos. This is why women bake and separate challah for Shabbos, a custom he says is still best kept at home rather than buying bakery challah.

title.en: Souls from the limbs of Adam, each with its shlichus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains from the Midrash that souls come from the head, heart, hands and feet of Adam HaRishon, so tzaddikim differ: some are devoted to Torah, some to tefilah, some to chesed and mitzvos. With free choice the same root can be used for other things, and a person finds his main avodah over time, with Hashem leading him like a father holding a child's hand.

title.en: The order of the generations as one body

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every generation contains a whole structure of Adam HaRishon, and so does the whole order of generations, like a fern whose every leaf is a small fern. The head is the generation of Moshe Rabbeinu and the desert, the heart is Dovid HaMelech who gave tefilah, and the generations descend until our own, which the Arizal and the Chofetz Chaim already called the heel.

title.en: The heel that feels nothing

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the heel, the bottom of the foot, as almost without feeling: a needle in the face hurts, in the heel it is barely felt, and the heel stays dark even under the summer sun. Hashem made it so that a person can walk; so too our generation has lost the sensitivity to Yiddishkeit, and our avodah is to be Jews even in that state.

title.en: Ikvesa dimeshicha and the distance from Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara at the end of Sotah on ikvesa dimeshicha and explains it as the heel of the generations, hoping it will turn over with Moshiach. The same order exists in place: Yerushalayim is head and heart of the world, and the exile has pushed Jews ever further away, from Bavel to Europe, America and Los Angeles.

title.en: Adar: hester within hester

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts earlier times, when tzaddikim showed wonders and Elul brought trembling, with today, when Yiddishkeit is mostly holiday foods and little is felt. He explains that the year ends with Adar, the month of hester panim, that today is hester within hester, and through the Baal Shem Tov's parable of the hiding father he explains the joy of Purim as finding Hashem within the hiding.

catalogTitle: מגילה - הוראה שבתוך ההסתר יש גילוי

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Megillah teaches how to find Hashem, whose name is hidden in it, behind the natural events of the world and of one's own life.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the order of the months: Nissan brings open miracles, while Adar, from the word for a cloak, holds miracles covered by nature. A mashal from the Bnei Yissaschar, of a dying man saved when the medicine from the East and the only doctor from the West arrive at the same moment, shows such a hidden miracle. The Megillah is full of such exact timings, yet Hashem's name never appears in it, which raises the question of how one says the brachah on its miracles. The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that 'the king' in the Megillah means Hashem: the erratic Achashverosh was only a puppet on strings. The name is not written openly because, as Rashi teaches, Hashem's name and throne are incomplete while Amalek, who brings doubt in emunah, exists. Still, the name is hidden in the verses, and learning the Megillah means searching for it. So too one must find Hashem in the news, in history and in one's own daily miracles; this is Purim.

en: Nissan is the month of open miracles, while the miracles of Adar are just as real but cloaked in nature.
The Megillah is built of exact timings, each adding a component to the miracle, which shows a guiding Hand rather than chance.
Following the Midrash, 'the king' in the Megillah means Hashem, since Achashverosh was a puppet moved by strings from above.
Hashem's name is not openly in the Megillah because His name and throne are incomplete while Amalek, the source of doubt in emunah, exists.
Learning the Megillah means searching for Hashem's name hidden between its lines, and then finding Him the same way in the news, in history and in one's own life.
The joy of Purim is the joy of finding Hashem in the midst of His hiddenness.

title.en: Adar: miracles under a cloak

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the open miracles of Nissan with those of Adar, a word he links to a cloak, which are covered by nature. He tells the Bnei Yissaschar's mashal of a dying man saved when a ship with the medicine from the East and a ship with the only doctor from the West arrive at once.

title.en: A Megillah of exact timings without Hashem's name

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that the Megillah is full of events falling at just the right moment, and ties Esther to the Gemara's hint of hester, hiddenness, at the end of the exile of Bavel. He then asks why Hashem's name is absent from the whole Megillah, where everything is natural, and how one can say the brachah on its miracles.

title.en: 'The king' means Hashem: the puppet Achashverosh

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that 'the king' in the Megillah refers to Hashem, and shows from Achashverosh's swings, with his wives, his advisors and his taxes, that he had no will of his own. He compares him to a marionette whose strings are pulled from above.

title.en: Amalek, doubt, and the incomplete name

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers with Rashi at the end of Parshas Beshalach that Hashem's name and throne are incomplete while Amalek exists. He explains how each person's deeds affect all creation, that Amalek, equal in gematria to safek, brings doubts in emunah, and that this is why the Megillah says 'the king' and not the name.

title.en: Searching for the hidden name, in the Megillah and in the news

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows Hashem's name hidden in the verses, at the roshei teivos of 'yavo hamelech veHaman hayom' and backwards in 'zeh einenu shoveh li', and says learning the Megillah means searching for it. He applies this to world leaders as puppets, to an x-ray that only a specialist can read, and to the fall of communism, telling what the Stoliner Rebbe said about it decades earlier.

title.en: The whole world is a Megillah: the joy of finding Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that the whole world, history and one's own life are a Megillah in which Hashem must be found, as the daily thanks in Modim says. With the picture of a disguised guest at the Purim seudah and the Ba'al Shem Tov's hide-and-seek, he describes the joy of finding Hashem inside the hiddenness, which is Purim.

catalogTitle: סיפורים מהחפץ חיים זצ”ל; נסיון דורנו - אמונה

oneLiner.en: Through the Chofetz Chaim's words after a dibbuk was driven out in Radin, the Mashgiach explains that open wonders were taken away so that the test of the last generation before Moshiach would be emunah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by explaining what a dibbuk is: a soul so stained by sin that it is not even admitted into Gehinnom to be cleansed, and that is pursued by destroying angels until it takes shelter in a living body. He then tells the famous story of a girl in Radin possessed by a dibbuk, whom Reb Elchonon Wasserman freed as the Chofetz Chaim's messenger. Along the way he tells of a young man cured of epilepsy through the Chofetz Chaim's forty-day fast, who lost the cure when he broke his promise of secrecy. Afterwards the Chofetz Chaim said there would be no more dibbukim until Moshiach, because in the generation of ikvesa diMeshicha the main test is emunah. The Mashgiach explains that this test belongs to our generation as a whole, compares it to the earlier test of tzitzis in the Divrei Chaim's time, and ends with kashrus, heretical reading and the pollution of the world.

en: A dibbuk is a soul too stained by sin to be admitted even into Gehinnom, which flees the destroying angels by entering a living body.
After the dibbuk in Radin was driven out, the Chofetz Chaim said there would be no more dibbukim until Moshiach, because such open sights make believing too easy.
The main test of the generation of ikvesa diMeshicha is emunah: to believe simply, without seeing wonders or proofs.
A seeker can recognize his own life's test by what is hard for him yet draws his desire; for our generation as a whole, that is emunah.
In the Divrei Chaim's time the Satan's effort was aimed at tzitzis; today it is aimed at emunah.
Kosher food preserves emunah, while heretical books and media poison it; the pollution of the physical world mirrors the pollution in the spiritual world.

title.en: What a dibbuk is

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the Chofetz Chaim's dibbuk story, which Reb Elchonon Wasserman used to retell yearly, and explains Gehinnom as a cleansing of the soul. Souls too stained even for Gehinnom wander the world chased by destroying angels and take refuge in a living body, bringing their bad traits with them.

title.en: The dibbuk in the girl from Radin

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how a girl in Radin fell ill and a man's voice spoke from her; the Chofetz Chaim sent Reb Elchonon Wasserman as his messenger. The dibbuk exposed people's sins, praised the Mashgiach's rebbe Reb Yisroel Chaim Kaplan, said the Chofetz Chaim is reckoned in Heaven as a Tanna, and explained that it entered her when she drank water without a brachah.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim's hidden forty-day fast

summary.en: As an aside the Mashgiach tells of a young man with epilepsy whom the Chofetz Chaim sent to a nearby rav for a brachah; he was cured and promised to tell no one. Years later he revealed it to a sick relative, fell ill again, and the Chofetz Chaim told him the cure had come from his own forty-day fast, which he no longer had the strength to repeat.

title.en: The dibbuk leaves; no more until Moshiach

summary.en: The dibbuk asks that the Chofetz Chaim learn mishnayos for it, and Reb Elchonon orders it out through the girl's little toe; the toe bursts, the window glass cracks and she recovers. The Chofetz Chaim then says there will be no more dibbukim until Moshiach, since such sights make emunah easy, while the test of ikvesa diMeshicha is emunah.

title.en: Emunah: the test of our generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach says wonders of tzaddikim are now rare, like lightning at night, because permission to show them was taken away. He mentions the dispute among Rishonim whether emunah is counted as a mitzvah, calls it the foundation of the Torah, and explains that the heel generation must believe simply; a seeker knows his test by what is hard for him yet desired, and for the generation as a whole that is emunah.

title.en: From tzitzis then to emunah now

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Divrei Chaim's responsa ruling machine-made tzitzis invalid, since a machine cannot act lishmah, and Rebbe Reb Elimelech's saying that the test of his generation was tzitzis; he digresses on machine matzos and Reb Yonasan Steif. Then the Satan's effort moved from tzitzis to emunah; the Mashgiach closes with kosher food as a preserver of emunah, heretical reading as its poison, and the polluted world as a mirror of the spiritual state at the end of galus.

catalogTitle: חרות על הלוחות - Free Yourself from the Bondages of your יצר הרע

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches young bachurim that Shavuos, the fiftieth day like the Yovel year, proclaims true freedom: freedom from slavery to the yetzer hara, which a person receives anew each year by preparing to accept the Torah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the eved Ivri, the Jewish slave who goes free in his seventh year but may choose to stay a slave, until the shofar of the fiftieth year, Yovel, frees everyone. In the same way, the Ramban explains that leaving Mitzrayim was only freedom from physical labor; the Jews became truly free fifty days later, at Har Sinai. The Mashgiach then shows what slavery really is through a seventeen-year-old who celebrates his eighteenth birthday with a pack of cigarettes, thinking he is free, while he is a slave to his yetzer hara; the same holds for late-night television and the internet. Charus al haluchos: the Luchos give freedom, but Shavuos needs preparation more than any other day, from the counting to Akdamus. A story of the Sanzer Rav's son shows that Matan Torah can be seen again. Shavuos is no commemoration like the Fourth of July: every year Hashem gives the Torah anew, and each person must receive it.

en: Just as the Yovel shofar frees every eved Ivri, even the one who wanted to stay a slave, the fiftieth day of Shavuos is the day of freedom for the Jewish people.

Following the Ramban, the Mashgiach explains that leaving Mitzrayim ended only physical bondage; true freedom means returning to the level of the Avos with the Shechinah upon them, reached fifty days later.
A person who does what his yetzer hara demands, against his own logic and his neshamah, is a slave, however free he imagines himself to be.
Charus al haluchos: the Luchos received on the fiftieth day are what give a person freedom.
No day in the Jewish calendar requires as much preparation as Shavuos, and the preparation runs from the counting through the night of learning to Akdamus.
Shavuos is not a commemoration like the Fourth of July: every year Hashem gives the Torah anew, and each person must do his part of kabbalas haTorah.
Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah for ruchniyus, a day of judgment for Torah, tefillah and middos, just as Rosh Hashanah in Tishrei is for gashmiyus.

title.en: The eved Ivri who refuses freedom

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises the bachurim for gathering to prepare for Shavuos, then turns to the parshiyos of Shemitah and Yovel: the eved Ivri goes free in his personal seventh year, his Shabbos, yet one wretched slave declares he wants to stay in chains.

title.en: Yovel, the Ramban and the fiftieth day

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the shofar of Yovel on Yom Kippur frees even the slave who wanted to stay. He brings the Ramban that leaving Mitzrayim was only freedom from physical labor, and that the Jews became free fifty days later; Sefirah parallels Shemitah and Yovel, and the shofar at Har Sinai proclaimed their freedom.

title.en: The boy who celebrates freedom with cigarettes

summary.en: To explain what freedom means, the Mashgiach describes a seventeen-year-old who is not allowed to smoke and on his eighteenth birthday flashes a pack of cigarettes as proof he is free. Pointing to the Surgeon General's warning and the years smokers lose, he shows that the boy is really a slave to his yetzer hara, fooling himself that one cigarette does no harm.

title.en: The crying neshamah: television and internet

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew's neshamah comes from heaven and protests inside him after an aveirah, but the slave of the yetzer hara cannot listen. He illustrates this with a boy kept up watching television until late at night instead of chazering, and with another who logs onto the internet and is dragged into filth while his yetzer tov begs him to break free.

title.en: Charus al haluchos and preparing for Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah in Pirkei Avos, charus al haluchos, read on the Shabbos before Shavuos: the Luchos received on the fiftieth day give freedom. He stresses that no day requires as much preparation as Shavuos and lists the stages: counting fifty days, the three days of preparation, staying up the night of Shavuos, and Akdamus, a lesson in emunah, before the Aseres Hadibros are heard.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav's son sees Matan Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Rav Chatzkel of Shinava, son of the Divrei Chaim of Sanz, spent Shavuos with Rav Shalom of Belz and beheld Matan Torah at the reading of the Torah. The next year his father kept him home and showed it to him himself, explaining that he had held back so his son would grow to see it with his own strength.

title.en: Matan Torah every year, not a commemoration

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one who believes it will feel that every Shavuos gives the Torah anew, and distinguishes Matan Torah from kabbalas haTorah, which depends on a person's desire. Contrasting the Fourth of July, a mere commemoration, he explains that Shavuos is a yearly rerun of Matan Torah and a Rosh Hashanah for ruchniyus, urges preparation through learning and davening, and closes with a brachah for true freedom.

catalogTitle: ע"י אמונה מקרבין הגאולה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach reads the Vilna Gaon's tradition that the parshiyos of Sefer Devarim match the centuries of the sixth millennium, finds the Holocaust in Vayeilech and the coming geulah in Nitzavim, and teaches that emunah is what will bring Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that every generation has its own mission, and the mission of the generation before Moshiach is emunah, which is harder now that the open wonders of tzaddikim are rare. He then brings the tradition of the Vilna Gaon's students that the ten parshiyos of Devarim correspond to the ten centuries of the sixth millennium, with the Gaon's own hint in Ki Seitzei, and notes that this places 5750 at the midday of the 'erev Shabbos' of history. He explains why earlier dates for Moshiach passed: they were times of eis ratzon that were not merited, and such missed moments can even turn into prosecution, as in 1914. Walking through Vayeilech, he finds the hester panim of the Holocaust, which began in 5700, and recalls the outbreak of the war from his own childhood. Nitzavim speaks of teshuvah and ingathering. He asks why the refuah precedes the makah and why they are two parshiyos, answers from the Gemara in Megillah and a surgeon parable, and closes that emunah will give Moshiach his strength.

en: The Mashgiach says the special mission of the generation before Moshiach is the mitzvah of emunah, the foundation of all mitzvos.
Following the Vilna Gaon, the ten parshiyos of Sefer Devarim match the ten centuries of the sixth millennium, so the present century corresponds to Nitzavim-Vayeilech.
Moshiach can come any day, but there are special times of eis ratzon (pekidos); if the generation does not merit them they pass, and they can even turn into a prosecution.
The hester panim of Vayeilech describes the first half of the current century, the Holocaust that began in 5700, and Nitzavim describes the teshuvah and redemption of its second half.
Emunah will be Moshiach's belt of strength, giving him the power to be revealed.

title.en: Emunah, the mission of this generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that every individual and generation has its own mission, and says that the mission of the generation before Moshiach is emunah. Since open wonders of tzaddikim are now rare, one must believe through the mesorah received from the fathers and by binding oneself to Torah and mitzvos.

title.en: The Gaon's ten parshiyos and ten centuries

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Vilna Gaon's teaching that the parshiyos of Devarim match the centuries of the sixth millennium, and the Gaon's hint to himself in Ki Seitzei when Rav Chaim Volozhiner asked him. By this count 5750 is midday of the 'erev Shabbos' of history, and the Gaon's students point to it for the geulah; he then asks why such dates matter when the dates of earlier gedolim passed.

title.en: Times of eis ratzon and their danger

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Moshiach can come any day, but there are hidden times of eis ratzon, called pekidos, that pass if the generation is not worthy, unlike the fixed time 'be'itah' that is never revealed. A missed eis ratzon can turn into a prosecution by the Satan, as happened in 1914, a year for which Moshiach had been calculated and in which the World War broke out.

title.en: Vayeilech and the outbreak of the war

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the Gaon's count to the current century, Nitzavim-Vayeilech, and tells how as a boy on the eve of 5700 he heard confident talk that Hitler would be crushed in days, and saw the congregation weeping on Rosh Hashanah. The war lasted years and six million were killed; he finds this first half of the century in the hester panim of Vayeilech.

title.en: Nitzavim: teshuvah and ingathering

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the second part, Nitzavim, as the promise of the century's second half: return to Hashem, ingathering from the farthest ends and the circumcision of the heart. He sees a drizzle, not yet a storm, of teshuvah today, and then asks two questions: why the redemption precedes the suffering in the order of the parshiyos, and why one parsha is two sidros.

title.en: Refuah before makah; emunah brings Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers both questions from the Gemara in Megillah that Hashem prepares the cure before He strikes Yisrael, illustrated with a surgeon who lays out bandages before cutting, and explains that the geulah will be so different that the suffering will seem like a dream. He hopes the geulah begins in 5750 and closes that emunah, Moshiach's belt in the haftarah, will give him the strength to be revealed.

catalogTitle: כל התיקון תלוי בהמתנה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that the whole tikkun of the world depends on waiting, and that our generation, in the footsteps of Moshiach, is living through the last test, the test of the Akeidah, where Hashem feels distant and the answers are hidden.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the idea that the test of our generation is emunah, and that a Jew must wait for Moshiach even if it takes long. The sin of Adam HaRishon was not waiting: the Tree of Knowledge was a vine whose wine he was meant to use for Kiddush on Friday night, and he ate before Shabbos. The sin of the Golden Calf was the same failure to wait, and the mitzvah of orlah teaches the same lesson. The Malbim's parable of the cookie shows that the maskilim 'know better' only because they need not wait. A letter of Rav Hillman and the two kinds of keitz lead to the call to keep believing. The Mashgiach then explains that a nisayon is meant to raise a person, and asks why the Akeidah, Avraham's tenth test, was harder than Ur Kasdim. His answer: at the Akeidah Avraham saw Hashem 'from afar', in a state of katnus, full of questions. By the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, our generation faces that same last test.

en: The Mashgiach says the test of our generation is emunah, and a Jew must wait and hope for Moshiach even if it takes a long time.
Adam HaRishon's sin was that he did not wait to use the Tree of Knowledge in holiness on Shabbos, and the sin of the Golden Calf was likewise a failure to wait.
The Mashgiach explains that a nisayon is meant to raise a person up, like a test that leads to promotion, so Avraham's ten tests grew harder until the Akeidah.
The Akeidah was the hardest test because Avraham then saw Hashem 'from afar', in a state of katnus, and had questions he could not answer.

By the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, the Jewish people's last test, in the footsteps of Moshiach, is the test of the Akeidah: Hashem feels distant and the answer is not known until Moshiach comes.

He explains that Adam's sin was eating from the Tree of Knowledge on Erev Shabbos instead of waiting to make Kiddush with its wine, that the Golden Calf was the same failure to wait, and he brings orlah as a lesson in waiting.

title.en: The Malbim: the maskilim need not wait

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Malbim's battles with the maskilim and his surprising remark that they 'know better' than him, explained with a parable of a cookie he may not eat on waking until he washes, davens and makes a brachah. A Jew must wait; that is all of Yiddishkeit.

title.en: Rav Hillman's letter and the two kitzin

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a short letter from Rav Hillman to Rav Pinchas Scheinberg, explaining that he had no time to write because he had to prepare for Moshiach. He says that even if an awaited time passes, Jews will keep believing, and he explains the two kitzin, 'b'itah' and 'achishenah'.

title.en: A nisayon is meant to raise

summary.en: The Mashgiach turns to the Akeidah, which is said daily and recalled in Selichos. From the two meanings of the root of 'nisah', to test and to raise up, he explains that every test is a promotion, so Avraham's ten tests grew harder; and he asks why the Akeidah should be the hardest, when any Jew would obey a direct prophecy.

title.en: Ur Kasdim versus the Akeidah: seeing Hashem from afar

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Ur Kasdim, where Avraham gave his life for a G-d he had never seen, with the Akeidah. He answers that at the Akeidah Avraham saw Hashem 'from afar': he was in katnus, without his usual feeling, and had questions on Hashem's promise about Yitzchak. The simple answer the angel later gave did not occur to him, because not knowing the answer is part of the test.

title.en: Our generation lives the test of the Akeidah

summary.en: Bringing the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the Avos are a sign for their children, the Mashgiach concludes that the Jewish people's last test mirrors the Akeidah: Hashem feels remote and there are questions, as in the books written after the Holocaust. The answer is simple and will be understood when Moshiach comes.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that the main task of our generation is to hold on to emunah, and that through simple faith, without saying 'if only', a small generation can reach its tikkun easily.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that the main task of our generation is to hold on to emunah, which is easily forgotten in a test. Dovid HaMelech, cursed by Shimi ben Gera, said 'Hashem told him to curse' and thereby became a leg of the Divine chariot. A story handed down from tzaddikim tells of souls who kept failing in gilgul after gilgul until Hashem gave them one mitzvah that includes all: emunah, on condition that they never say 'volt', 'if only'. The Mashgiach explains 'volt' as denial of hashgachah pratis. In the heels of Moshiach the world, physically and spiritually polluted, makes avodah hard, and emunas chachamim is part of emunah: the machlokes of an earlier generation delayed Moshiach, so today one should keep silent. Through the Maharsham's story, where Torah learned even not for its own sake was saved in heaven, he shows that little is expected of us, and urges not to despair.

en: The Mashgiach says the main task of this generation is to hold on to emunah, which a person easily forgets when a test comes.
Saying 'volt', 'if only I had done otherwise', is a flaw in emunah, because everything, down to what one manages to buy, is determined from Heaven.
In the heels of Moshiach the world is polluted both physically and spiritually, so every act of avodah is harder and requires more effort.
Emunas chachamim and emunas tzaddikim are part of emunah in Hashem; taking sides in disputes of the gedolim pushes off Moshiach, and the Mashgiach says one should keep silent.
Hashem measures our generation by other standards and expects of it only what can be expected; through emunah it will become the generation of Moshiach.

Sent ever higher, they reached Hashem, who gave them one mitzvah that includes all 613, emunah, on condition that they never say 'volt'.

title.en: 'Volt', hashgachah pratis and a polluted world

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'volt' with the example of an item sold minutes before one arrived, a shidduch, business and an esrog, and says everything is hashgachah pratis. One who believes without 'volt' already has his tikkun in the heels of Moshiach. He shows that today's physical pollution mirrors a spiritual one that makes Torah, tefillah and emunas chachamim hard.

title.en: Machlokes that delays Moshiach; silence and emunah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer's words that the great generation before him could have brought Moshiach, but the masses turned the machlokes between Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz and Rabbi Yaakov Emden into rechilus. He warns that taking sides today delays Moshiach, compares an opinion on the Kleve get from a tailor, and says one should keep silent and believe. Like the generation of Mitzrayim, our small generation will become great.

title.en: The Maharsham before the heavenly court

summary.en: From the introduction to Techeles Mordechai the Mashgiach tells how the young Maharsham fell gravely ill and his family sent a kvitel to Rabbi Eizikl. The Maharsham later told that in Heaven a black angel blew his Torah off the scale as not lishmah, until a new dayan from the earthly court cried out that in such times even Torah not lishmah is precious, and he was judged for life.

title.en: The Rebbe was the dayan; no despair

summary.en: The Mashgiach finishes the story: the Maharsham recovered at the hour of the bracha, and when he came to thank the Rebbe he recognized him as the dayan who had saved him; by tradition the Rebbe asked him always to be lenient, and Rabbi Chaim defended his rulings. The Mashgiach concludes that our generation is measured by other standards, no one should despair, and through emunah it will become the generation of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: Preparing for the Day when one's Spiritual Destiny is Determined

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah for the Torah life of a Jew, a day of freedom, renewal and a wedding with Hashem, and that it demands more preparation than any other day of the year.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that calls Shavuos a Rosh Hashanah, and with the Ramban that the Jews were not called redeemed until Matan Torah. Using a parable of a young man who thinks smoking makes him free, he shows that real freedom is release from the yetzer hara, the theme of Yovel and of the fiftieth day. Every Yom Tov is a reliving, not a commemoration, so on Shavuos the heavens open again, as a son of the Sanzer Rav saw. Hence the long preparation: Sefirah, teshuvah, the mikveh, the night of learning, even Akdamus. Shavuos is a day to become a new Jew, like Yisro and Rus. The Shabbos before feeds the Yom Tov. Shavuos is a chuppah: one must not sleep through it, the night's Tanach adorns the kallah, and the morning mikveh carries great holiness. He closes that Shavuos is a decisive day and a meeting with Hashem.

en: Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah, and the Mashgiach says one should treat it as a new start.
True freedom is not doing whatever one wants but being free of the yetzer hara; that freedom came on the fiftieth day, with the Torah.
A Yom Tov is not a commemoration like the Fourth of July; the original event returns each year on its day.
No event in the year requires as much preparation as Shavuos: Sefirah, teshuvah, removing every barrier, the night of learning, the davening and Akdamus.
Shavuos is the chuppah between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and after all the preparation one must not miss the chuppah itself by sleeping through the davening and the reading of the Torah.
Shavuos is a decisive day on which a person receives the Torah and his avodah for the whole year.

title.en: Shavuos as a Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that calls Shavuos a Rosh Hashanah and says one should start anew. He notes that the Jews went through a complete change between Mitzrayim and Matan Torah, and cites the Ramban that they were not called redeemed until they received the Torah.

title.en: Freedom from the yetzer hara

summary.en: Through a parable of an eighteen-year-old who buys cigarettes to show he is free, the Mashgiach shows that such a person is a slave to his yetzer hara. He ties true freedom to the luchos in Pirkei Avos, to Shemitah and Yovel, and to the fiftieth day of Sefirah, when the Jews became free servants of Hashem.

title.en: A Yom Tov is relived, not commemorated

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the year to a rotating card file of 365 cards: what happened on a day is engraved on its card and returns with it. Unlike the Fourth of July, which only commemorates, the fifteenth of Nisan and Shavuos bring back their original light.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav's son sees Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a son of the Sanzer Rav who traveled to Belz for Shavuos and saw the heavens open at the reading of the Torah, and how his father showed him the same in Sanz only after he had worked on himself. From this he says one must believe that one receives a share in the Torah on Shavuos, and must prepare through the days of Sefirah.

title.en: Teshuvah, mikveh and the night before

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how Rashi knows that the Jews arrived at Sinai with teshuvah, and answers that one cannot come to Sinai without it, and that their unity there proves it. He describes Shavuos as a mikveh that requires removing every barrier, the night of learning, the long davening of the tzaddikim and Akdamus as one preparation after another.

title.en: Becoming a new Jew on Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions a Midrash Peliah and offers a simple explanation: Shavuos is a time to turn a new leaf, as if until now one was not a Jew. He points to Yisro and Rus, both converts, and to the Yid HaKadosh of Peshischa, for whom every day was a new becoming a Jew.

title.en: The Shabbos before Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the six weekdays are blessed from Shabbos, and that this is why the parsha of the Yamim Tovim in Emor opens with Shabbos: each Yom Tov draws from the Shabbos before it. He urges using the Shabbos before Shavuos, and mentions the Zohar on the night of Shavuos.

title.en: Shavuos is a chuppah: don't sleep through it

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Shavuos as the chuppah between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, citing the piyutim and the last Mishnah in Taanis. With a parable of a chassan who prepares for weeks and then stays home from his own chuppah, he criticizes staying up all night only to sleep through the davening and the reading of the Torah, and tells of a Rebbe who sent his tired chassidim to sleep so they could daven well.

title.en: The night of Tanach adorns the kallah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that staying up on Shavuos night comes from the Zohar: the Torah is a kallah with twenty-four ornaments, matching the twenty-four books of Tanach, as Rashi brings, and the twenty-four arrangements of the Name of Adnus. He then raises a difficulty on the Chok Yaakov about the Mishnayos in the Tikkun.

title.en: The mikveh on Shavuos morning

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the great holiness of the mikveh at daybreak on Shavuos, explains that a mikveh has levels set by halachah, and tells of a holy man who could feel by touch whether a mikveh was kosher. He brings the Arizal on the Shavuos morning tevilah and says the tzaddikim sang as they went to the mikveh.

title.en: A decisive day and a meeting with Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that Shavuos decides a person's Torah and avodah for the year. He brings the Chiddushei HaRim that Moshe taught the Jews the content of each Yom Tov, and explains that every regel, and Shavuos most of all, is a meeting with Hashem, for which one must come prepared and dressed in mitzvos.

catalogTitle: חבירים טובים; ליצנות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that before the geulah the Satan fights for his life against emunah, and that his two sharpest weapons today are bad friends and leitzanus, mockery.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Jews in Mitzrayim believed Moshe at first but no longer listened to him shortly before the redemption. Answering in the name of the Satmar Rav, he explains that just before a geulah the Satan throws all his strength against emunah, the foundation of Yiddishkeit, since he knows Moshiach will end him; like anyone fighting for his life he gains new strength. The Mishnah's miracle that the Kohen Gadol never became tamei on Yom Kippur shows the same thing, as the Tosfos Yom Tov explains, and so does a candle that flares up before it goes out. Today's war is fought through bad friends: the Rambam says a person must flee even to the desert to escape them, and the Chazon Ish named the yeshiva as today's refuge. The Satan now bites with a kiss, like Esav, through friendship and assimilation. A story of the Lechovitcher Rebbe shows the power of good friends, and the Mashgiach closes on leitzanus, which overturns logic and keeps a person from greeting the Shechinah.

en: Just before a geulah the greatest test is in emunah, because the Satan, knowing his end is near, throws all his strength against it.
Whoever fights for his life gains new strength, and so the Satan fights hardest in the generation of Moshiach.
Among the greatest dangers to Yiddishkeit in this generation are bad friends, who reach even into the yeshiva.
The Satan's tactic today is friendship rather than hatred, biting with a kiss, and it has brought many Jews to assimilation.
Good friends can accomplish what neither geonim nor rebbes can, so a person must choose his friends with care.
Leitzanus is the opposite of logic: one jest pushes away a hundred rebukes, and leitzim do not greet the Shechinah.

He brings the Mishnah's miracle that the Kohen Gadol never became tamei on Yom Kippur, and the Tosfos Yom Tov's explanation that the Satan concentrated all his power on him.

title.en: The flaring candle and the danger of bad friends

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the Satan to a candle that flares up before it goes out, which is why it is so hard to be a Jew today. He names bad friends as one of the generation's greatest dangers, brings the Rambam that one must flee them even to the desert, and the Chazon Ish's answer to the Satmar Rav that today one flees to the yeshiva, which itself still needs guarding.

title.en: Biting with a kiss: the Satan's tactic today

summary.en: From the dotted word 'vayishakehu' and the Midrash that Esav meant to bite Yaakov, the Mashgiach shows that the Satan now bites with a kiss. Where the nations once persecuted the Jews, today they offer friendship and interfaith gatherings, and assimilation reaches even observant homes through gentile books, newspapers and radio, poisoning emunah.

title.en: The Lechovitcher chassid saved by his friends

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a chassid of the Lechovitcher Rebbe who faced a great temptation on the road and was held back only by the thought that his fellow chassidim would drag him to the Rebbe. The Rebbe told him that good friends can accomplish what neither geonim nor rebbes can.

title.en: Leitzanus, the opposite of logic

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls leitzanus one of the great pitfalls: a jealous bochur mocks one who learns well, and one jest pushes away a hundred rebukes, as a child's quip once undid a whole talk of Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz. He explains that a joke is the opposite of logic, so no argument can answer it, brings the Gemara that leitzim do not greet the Shechinah, and closes that whoever wants to see Moshiach needs good friends and must keep away from leitzim.

catalogTitle: עשה לך רב

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah left its measures vague so that a Jew must keep turning to a rav and so cleave to talmidei chachamim, his main advice for holding on in the trials of emunah before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach returns to the advice for the trials before Moshiach: make yourself a rav and cling to rebbeim and good friends, as the best talmidim of Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz did. Faith in the sages is part of emunah, as the passuk joins faith in Hashem with faith in Moshe. He brings the Gemara that the seven species praising Eretz Yisrael teach the Torah's shiurim, shows that nearly every halachah depends on them, and how unclear they are. The Torah left them vague so that a Jew must keep coming to the rav and cleave to talmidei chachamim. Turning to today's trial of emunah, he explains through the word 'tevel' that the world is dark and confused, lit only by flashes. He tells stories of hidden insight from Slonim and of the Yeshuos Yaakov, and closes that one sees wonders today by reflecting on the Jews in Eretz Yisrael.

en: In the trials before Moshiach, the Mashgiach says, one of the main pieces of advice is to make oneself a rav and to stay close to rebbeim and good friends.
Just as one must believe in Hashem, one must believe that the sages of each generation are His messengers to lead the Jewish people.
Almost every halachah in the Torah depends on shiurim, measures learned from the seven species, yet those measures are far from clear.
The Torah did not give exact measures so that a Jew would constantly have to go to the rav, and through this cleave to talmidei chachamim.
Today's trial of emunah is that open wonders are rare; the world is 'tevel', a confused darkness lit only by Hashem's occasional flashes.
Even now one can see wonders by reflecting on current events, above all the survival of the Jews in Eretz Yisrael among their enemies.

title.en: Why the Torah left the measures vague

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah, given to a people who could build with precision, measured by the hand and finger. He answers that the Torah wants a Jew to keep coming to the rav, cleaving to talmidei chachamim, until the chacham becomes his guide in all of life.

title.en: Tevel: a confused world lit by flashes

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes today's trial of emunah: there are great tzaddikim but few open wonders. He explains the world's name 'tevel' from Rashi as a confusion, like a dark night in the country, and says that even in hester panim Hashem's lightning flashes light up the confused world.

title.en: Stories from Slonim: the beard and the knife

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells stories he heard from a Slonimer chassid and others: the Slonimer Rebbe, the Beis Avraham, in Yerushalayim, who taught a shaven simple Jew and a learned chassid the difference between them, and the Rebbe's gabbai who knew that a new knife had not been toiveled.

title.en: The Yeshuos Yaakov's cake; wonders today

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells from seforim how the Yeshuos Yaakov delayed the brachah on a cake with long pilpulim until it turned out to be forbidden, and how he denied it was ruach hakodesh. He closes that today emunah is demanded, and that one sees wonders by reflecting on the Jews in Eretz Yisrael.

catalogTitle: ביאור ברייתא בסוף מס' סוטה בענין עיקבתא דמשיחא

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach goes through the baraisa at the end of Sotah on the signs of the 'heels of Moshiach', shows each sign in his own time, and concludes that with no true leaders left a Jew can rely only on his Father in Heaven and must hold fast to emunah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the baraisa at the end of Sotah describing the time before Moshiach and applies its signs one by one. Chutzpah grows; prices rise even when supply is plentiful; the government turns to heresy, which he sees in the Russian state, whose seventy-year atheist rule is now crumbling, illustrated by a visit to Russian Jews who had forgotten almost all of Yiddishkeit. He continues with the loss of truth, the mocking of those who turn from evil, the breakdown of respect within the family, and the face of the generation like the face of a dog: leaders who walk in front but look back to see what the crowd wants. A parable of the shepherd and his dog shows that the last leaders will only hold the people together. With no leader of the stature of the Chofetz Chaim, he says, a Jew relies on his Father in Heaven. A wheat merchant's parable teaches that today mitzvos are not scrutinized, so one can earn much. He closes by stressing the mitzvah of emunah.

en: The baraisa's signs of the heels of Moshiach, rising chutzpah and prices that climb despite plentiful supply, are visible in the Mashgiach's own time.
'The kingdom will turn to heresy' was fulfilled for the first time in history by the Russian state, and its collapse is a sign that Moshiach is near.
The face of the generation is like the face of a dog: the leaders walk in front but look back to see what the community wants.
When there is no leader for the whole people, a Jew must not despair, because the same Ribono shel Olam who gave the Torah is present today.
In the time before Moshiach mitzvos are not scrutinized in Heaven, so it is a time when a person can earn a great deal.
The mitzvah of emunah, which the Mashgiach has been teaching for years from the Sefer Chareidim, is a person's lifeline in the heels of Moshiach.

title.en: Chutzpah, rising prices and a kingdom of heresy

He describes a recent visit to Russian Jews who had forgotten almost all of Yiddishkeit, and sees the breaking of that kingdom as a sign that Moshiach is near.

title.en: Truth missing, family broken, the dog's face

summary.en: The Mashgiach continues with the baraisa: impoverished border towns, the parallel Gemara in Sanhedrin where one who turns from evil is called mad, the absence of truth, and the young shaming the old, which he sees in the breakdown of the family. He explains 'the face of the generation like the face of a dog' with a man walking his dog: leaders walk in front but look back to see what the community wants, and avoid speaking about Shabbos, kashrus or Torah learning.

title.en: Shepherd and dog; leaders gone, rely on Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a parable of a shepherd who feeds his flock and a dog that only keeps it together: the last leaders before Moshiach will only hold the people together. He brings the passuk in Haazinu on 'none restrained or left', recalls the days of the Chofetz Chaim, the Gerrer Rebbe and the Chazon Ish, and concludes from the end of the baraisa that a Jew must not despair, for the same Ribono shel Olam is with him today.

title.en: The wheat merchant: no scrutiny in hard times

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a parable of a wheat merchant who was gloomy in times of plenty, when buyers inspected every grain, and cheerful in wartime, when hungry people took whatever he had. So too in the heels of Moshiach mitzvos are not scrutinized above, and one can earn much through Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

title.en: The mitzvah of emunah: the most important point

summary.en: The Mashgiach announces that next week he will reach the most important point of the whole zman. He describes how his learning of the Sefer Chareidim with bochurim came to center entirely on the mitzvah of emunah, how former students thank him for keeping them in Yiddishkeit, and he asks his listeners to take it seriously, closing with the navi's words about emunah and Moshiach.

catalogTitle: Rectifying the Months of תמוז and אב (connection to פרשת שלח)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tamuz and Av, the months of the meraglim and of strict judgment, are meant to be transformed, through guarding the eyes and remembering that each person is Hashem's shaliach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the letter combination of Tamuz, drawn from Haman's words 'v'chol zeh einenu shoveh li': fully reversed and from the final letters, it marks Tamuz as the hardest month, a month of strict judgment. Because it comes from the Megillah of 'v'nahapoch hu', the task is to transform it, and Chof-Gimmel Sivan, the day of the good news in the Megillah, falls this year on the Shabbos of blessing Tamuz. He touches on Parshas Shelach's challah and nesachim as the return of the kallah, then explains the meraglim: they went in days of judgment, and their delay for Miriam brought them back on Tisha B'Av, which holds the birth of Moshiach. Tamuz and Av are the two eyes; the meraglim blemished seeing, so these months bring trials of the eyes. Finally, everyone is Hashem's shaliach, and a person's name is his shlichus; summer vacation should be used to see Hashem in nature.

en: The letter combination of Tamuz comes from Haman's words in the Megillah, fully reversed and from the final letters, marking it as the hardest month of strict judgment, which must be transformed as in 'v'nahapoch hu'.
Chof-Gimmel Sivan, the day the good news of 'v'nahapoch hu' went out, falls on the Shabbos when Tamuz is blessed, a sign to use it to transform the month.
The meraglim went in days of strict judgment; waiting for Miriam brought their return to Tisha B'Av, which the Mashgiach calls a day with a good inner side, the birth of Moshiach.
Tamuz and Av are the two eyes; the meraglim blemished seeing, so these months carry the greatest trials of the eyes, and one who wants to stay bound to Hashem must guard his eyes in them.
Every person is a shaliach sent down by Hashem to bring up Torah and mitzvos, and his name carries his shlichus; the yetzer hara works to make him forget it.
The summer vacation should be used as Hashem wants, including seeing His creation in nature and coming through it to love and awe of Him, as the Rambam describes.

title.en: Tamuz, the hardest month

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the letter combination of Tamuz, from Haman's 'v'chol zeh einenu shoveh li', is fully reversed and from final letters, worse than Av's, so the whole month is judgment. He says the answer is not to sulk but to transform it, which is why its combination comes from the Megillah of 'v'nahapoch hu'.

title.en: Chof-Gimmel Sivan, a day of transformation

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions the custom not to make weddings after the twenty-second of the month, and that the Chiddushei HaRim and the Divrei Chaim made weddings on Chof-Gimmel Sivan because of its standing. It is the day the good news of 'v'nahapoch hu' went out, and this year it is the Shabbos of blessing Tamuz, a sign to use it to transform the month.

title.en: Challah and nesachim: the kallah returns

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Shelach a hard sedra of the meraglim but also a good one, with challah and nesachim. He brings the Zohar's parable of a king who sent his kallah away three times, the last time to a foul place, where he himself comes to bring her back, and connects nesachim and challah to the place of the Beis HaMikdash from which Adam and Chava were taken.

title.en: The meraglim in days of judgment

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the meraglim went in Tamuz and Av, days of judgment, bringing the Rema MiPano's reading of 'bikurei anavim' as hinting to the Satan, and adds that the Tamuz combination equals 'yemei bikurei anavim' in gematria. He brings the Satmar Rav that waiting for Miriam brought the return on Tisha B'Av, which turns out to be good, since it is the day of Moshiach's birth.

title.en: Mechiyas Amalek before every Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that wiping out Amalek precedes every building of the Mikdash: Amalek before the Mishkan, Shaul's war on Erev Pesach, Mordechai before the second Beis HaMikdash, and again before Moshiach. He then asks how Shaul could say 'hakimosi es dvar Hashem', and explains that by leaving Agag alive Haman came into the world, leading to Purim and 'kiymu v'kiblu'.

title.en: Why waiting for Miriam was a blessing

summary.en: In the same way, the Mashgiach asks what would have happened had they not waited for Miriam: the meraglim, sent on the twenty-ninth of Sivan, would have left on Chof-Gimmel Sivan and blemished that day forever. So the delay was a blessing, and Tamuz, rooted in lashon hara, must be transformed like Purim.

title.en: Tamuz and Av, the two eyes

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings, he thinks from the Bnei Yissaschar, that Tamuz and Av are the two eyes of the year, hinted in 'eini eini yordah mayim'. The meraglim blemished seeing, so these months bring the greatest trials of the eyes; he brings the Gemara in Bava Basra on one who shuts his eyes from evil and the Midrash on 'am naval', applying them to the streets today.

title.en: The two nesi'im of Tamuz and Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach matches the twelve nesi'im to the months: the two who sinned, Elitzur ben Shdeiur of Reuven in Korach's dispute and Shlumiel ben Tzurishaddai of Shimon, who was Zimri, belong to Tamuz and Av. 'Otzem einav me're'os bera' equals their names in gematria, and the eyes must be rectified until 'ayin b'ayin yiru'. He adds an unclear story of tears on Tisha B'Av and a word on holding the Kiddush cup like a rose.

title.en: Summer travel and our shlichus

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that everyone travels in Tamuz and Av, a season of sending, and brings the Chasam Sofer that both Hashem and the people sent the meraglim. Every person is a shaliach: the neshamos sang above until Hashem sent them down to bring up the gems of Torah and mitzvos, yet people rushing in the street forget who sent them.

title.en: A person's name is his shlichus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the angel of Esav would not tell Yaakov his name: a person's name is his shlichus, which is why one says a passuk of his name after Shemoneh Esrei. The yetzer hara wants people to forget their name and their mission, so he urges a cheshbon hanefesh this Shabbos and to say one is the shaliach of Hashem alone.

title.en: Using the vacation to see Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach takes leave until after the summer and tells the bochurim to use the vacation as Hashem wants: exercise and swimming are fine, but it is no time to throw off the yoke. In the city tall buildings block the sky, while in the country one should look at trees, streams and butterflies and come, as the Rambam writes, to love of Hashem.

title.en: A tzaddik's last look at creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a great tzaddik who, in his last days in a Tel Aviv hospital, asked to be carried to the garden to see Hashem's creation once more, and of another who davened looking out at the fields. He closes with 'se'u marom eineichem', the Rambam on awe through creation, and blessings for a healthy summer and the great 'v'nahapoch hu'.

catalogTitle: זהירות בקדושה וכשרות המאכלים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the soul, like the body, loses its healthy appetite for Torah and emunah through forbidden food and through lapses in kedushah, and he teaches how to handle the doubts in emunah that come in their wake.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach compares the soul to a living organism: just as unhealthy food ruins the body's appetite, sins dull the heart, and forbidden food above all weakens a person's emunah. He supports this with a letter of the Rambam and with the Divrei Chaim's explanation of why German Jewry fell, and warns how hard kashrus is today, urging care about whose hechsher one relies on. The second cause of doubts is a lapse in kedushas Yisrael, guarding the eyes and thoughts. He explains that before Moshiach the power of Amalek, whose gematria equals safek, grows, so many sincere bochurim suffer doubts; their pain itself shows they believe. One must not argue with such thoughts, which are leitzanus rather than logic, but push them away; the Bnei Yissaschar says this fulfills the mitzvah of 'velo sasuru'. He closes by tying this to parshas Shelach and the summer travel season as a shlichus.

en: The soul is a spiritual organism: just as bad food ruins the body's appetite, sin dulls the heart and takes away the soul's natural desire for Torah, tefillah and Hashem's will.
Of all sins, eating forbidden food in particular causes a person to lose his emunah.
Kashrus today is very difficult, so one must know that the rav giving a hechsher is both a yerei shamayim and competent in the field.
The second cause of doubts in emunah is a lapse in kedushas Yisrael, guarding one's eyes and thoughts.
Doubts in emunah before Moshiach come from the strengthening of Amalek, and a person who suffers from them is not a non-believer; his very pain shows that he believes.
One must not argue with doubting thoughts or answer them with logic; one pushes them away and ignores them, and they will pass.

title.en: Forbidden food dulls the soul's appetite

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the soul to the body: unhealthy food ruins a person's appetite for good food, and sins take away the soul's natural desire for Torah and tefillah. He brings the Gemara that sin dulls the heart and says forbidden food above all causes a loss of emunah.

title.en: The Rambam, German Jewry and kashrus today

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a letter to the Rambam about techiyas hameisim, whose answer traced the questioners' weak emunah to forbidden food, and of the Divrei Chaim's explanation that German Jewry fell because its shochtim were not God-fearing. He then describes how hard kashrus is today with packaged ingredients, and says one may rely only on a hechsher of a rav known to be both a yerei shamayim and expert.

title.en: Kedushah, doubts and the power of Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach names the second cause of doubts: lack of care in kedushas Yisrael, from the passuk in the week's parsha about not straying after one's heart and eyes. He says many sincere bochurim come to him in tears over doubts, explains that before Moshiach Jews will enter the fiftieth gate of impurity, and that doubts come from Amalek, which equals safek in gematria.

title.en: Doubts before Moshiach are a test, not kefirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares today's spiritual atmosphere to physical pollution, and says the bochurim's tears over their doubts show they believe. He brings the Ohr Hameir and Reb Yisroel of Ruzhin on how hard emunah will be before Moshiach, and teaches that everyone faces such a period and should push the thought out like a fly that keeps returning.

title.en: Don't argue with the thoughts: 'velo sasuru'

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a man whom a tzaddik told to ignore a disturbing image during davening, and recalls his own shock as a bochur when a friend told Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz he had doubts. He explains that such thoughts are leitzanus, not logic, so they must be pushed away rather than answered, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar that pushing them out fulfills the mitzvah of 'velo sasuru', with a remez from its trop.

title.en: A private geulah and the summer as a shlichus

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every Jew should await his own redemption from a period of trials and emerge from it with clearer emunah, strengthening himself in Torah and tefillah and ignoring the doubts. He contrasts the meraglim of the parsha with Yehoshua's successful spies of the haftarah, calls the summer travels a shlichus that can repair the meraglim's forty days, and parts with wishes for a successful summer.

catalogTitle: ציפוי לגאולה ועניני משיח

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that hoping and waiting for Moshiach every day, even through disappointments, is the obligation of every Jew, the tikkun of Adam's sin, and a channel for all yeshuos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that a person is asked in Heaven whether he awaited the yeshuah, which includes the complete geulah. He shows this hope in Shemoneh Esrei and in the Rambam's principle that one awaits Moshiach every day. In times of trouble and war the hope should be sharper, with a cheshbon hanefesh. He says the events of the Holocaust and the founding of the State were not the geulah, that Hashem runs the world by His own plan, and that the disappointments were foretold by Yeshaya as birth pangs that bring forth nothing. The Ramban on Haazinu shows that the fulfilled prophecies guarantee the rest. All galus comes to repair Adam's sin of not waiting, repeated at the Golden Calf and by Shaul, while David waited. After the Malbim's story about waiting, he shows how waiting draws down yeshuos, and how the tefillos are full of this hope.

en: Every Jew is obligated to hope constantly for the yeshuah, which includes the complete geulah, as the Gemara, Shemoneh Esrei and the Rambam's principles show.
In times of trouble and war, when the signs point to Moshiach, a person should be more aroused and make a cheshbon hanefesh.
The disappointments of recent generations were not the geulah, but the navi already foretold such birth pangs that bring forth nothing.
The sin of Adam, repeated at the Golden Calf and by Shaul, was not waiting; the avodah of galus is to wait, and this repairs that sin.
By hoping for Moshiach, the root of all yeshuos, a Jew draws down personal yeshuos even now, and a Jew is measured by how much he hopes.

title.en: The question in Heaven: did you await the yeshuah?

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that a person is asked in Heaven whether he awaited the yeshuah, which includes the complete geulah. He shows this hope in the Shemoneh Esrei bracha of Es Tzemach David and in the Rambam's principle, condensed in Ani Maamin, that one awaits Moshiach every single day.

title.en: Heightened hope in times of trouble

summary.en: Although one must hope every day, the Mashgiach explains that when troubles and wars come, as Chazal describe, a person should be more aroused and ask himself whether he has learned and davened enough. He tells of Rav Moshe of Savran, who remembered every thought because for him every moment was like a wedding.

title.en: Not the geulah, and the great disappointment

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that what happened after the Holocaust and with the founding of the State was not the geulah or its beginning, but the opposite of what the Rambam describes. Hashem runs the world by His own plan, and a Jew's task is Torah and mitzvos, not politics. He describes the disappointment after the churban and after the miracles in Eretz Yisrael this year.

title.en: Birth pangs that bring forth nothing, and the Ramban on Haazinu

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Yeshaya, who compares the geulah to a birth preceded by pangs, and laments a woman who suffers and bears a stillborn child: the navi foresaw such disappointments. The end of Haazinu speaks of the geulah, and the Ramban argues that since the first part of the prophecy came true, the second part will surely come too.

title.en: Not waiting: from Adam to the Golden Calf and Shaul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that all galus comes to repair Adam's sin, which was not waiting until Shabbos, when the eitz hadaas would have become permitted. The Golden Calf was the same failure to wait for Moshe, and Shaul did not wait for Shmuel, while David waited for the sign and began the tikkun. Every Jew, a fragment of Adam, repairs his share by waiting.

title.en: The Malbim: a Jew knows how to wait

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Malbim, debating a maskil, described his morning: hungry, yet waiting through washing, davening, netilas yadayim, hamotzi and the salt before eating. From here he says the whole Shulchan Aruch is waiting, and so is Shabbos.

title.en: Waiting despite disappointment, and the joy when he comes

summary.en: Through the example of orlah the Mashgiach shows that a Jew's avodah is waiting, and that despite disappointments one keeps waiting, which repairs Adam's sin. He brings Chavakuk, Yeshaya and Tehillim on the reward of those who wait, and describes how, when Moshiach comes, Jews will point to Hashem and say this is the One we hoped for, and every minute of waiting will be a treasure.

title.en: Waiting draws down yeshuos; the power of amen

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that by waiting for the general yeshuah of Moshiach, the root of all yeshuos, one draws down healing and success even now, drawing water from its wellspring. He brings the Gemara that emunim are those who say amen: answering amen to a bracha about what one has not yet seen is belief, and Hashem stores these amens in His treasury.

title.en: Tefillos full of hope; the measure of a Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Jews never forget Yerushalayim because they know it will be rebuilt, and that Aleinu, Shemoneh Esrei, bentching and the Shabbos Kedushah are all hope and prayer for the geulah. He concludes that a Jew is measured by how much he hopes and longs for Moshiach, and that this longing itself brings the geulah closer.

catalogTitle: Transforming the Three Weeks

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Three Weeks are great days that have fallen, like the Nephilim, and that the task of these weeks is to lift them up and transform them, and oneself, through Torah, tefillah and emunah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by showing that Zimri was no ordinary sinner but Shlumiel ben Tzurishaddai, a Nasi and one of the seventy souls. From Parshas Shlach on, the parshiyos of Tammuz tell of great people who fell: the meraglim, Korach, Moshe at Mei Merivah, Zimri. The forty days of the meraglim, from Rosh Chodesh Tammuz to Tisha B'Av, are days of midas hadin. The meraglim met the Nephilim, angels cast down from heaven; since the Torah repeats itself in every generation, and Sefer Yetzirah teaches that time parallels place and soul, we meet Nephilim in time: the Three Weeks are lofty days that have fallen, destined to become the greatest festivals. The Mashgiach brings remazim, the Chozeh of Lublin, and the transformations of Lavan into Barzilai and of Balak into the ancestor of Moshiach, and calls on his listeners to dig out the hidden good, transform themselves, and above all daven, as Yehoshua and Kalev did.

en: Zimri was a distinguished tzaddik: Nasi of Shevet Shimon, one of the seventy souls, whose day in Nisan is still marked, and a family was named after him even after his sin.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Tammuz to Tisha B'Av are the days the meraglim spent in Eretz Yisrael, days of midas hadin, and their parshiyos tell of tzaddikim who turned sour.
The Torah is not a history book: what the meraglim met in place, the Nephilim, we meet in time during these forty days.
The Three Weeks are not low days but lofty days that have fallen, destined to become the most joyous days of the year.
The mission of the Three Weeks is to transform them from klala into bracha through extra Torah, tefillah and tzedakah, as Hashem turned Bilaam's curse into a blessing out of love.
Even Lavan, Bilaam and Balak had good at their core, which was later transformed into Barzilai and into Dovid HaMelech and Moshiach.
The missing ingredient by the meraglim was tefillah; Yehoshua and Kalev were saved because they had it.
