title.en: Who was Zimri?

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Pinchas and Zimri and asks who Zimri was. He shows from Chazal that Zimri was Shlumiel ben Tzurishaddai, Nasi of Shevet Shimon and one of the seventy souls who went down to Mitzrayim, whose day in Nisan is still marked by not saying Tachanun, and after whom a family was named even after his sin.

title.en: Tzaddikim who turned sour

summary.en: Contrasting the good guys and bad guys of his childhood stories with the Torah's tzaddikim and resha'im, the Mashgiach says that from Parshas Shlach, read on Shabbos Mevarchim Tammuz, a new figure appears: tzaddikim who fell. He explains that the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Tammuz to Tisha B'Av are the days of the meraglim, days of midas hadin.

title.en: Korach, Mei Merivah and Zimri

summary.en: The Mashgiach follows the pattern through the parshiyos of Tammuz: Korach, the greatest tzaddik of Shevet Levi according to the Zohar, who turned sour; the criticism of Moshe Rabbeinu at Mei Merivah in Chukas; and in Balak and Pinchas, Zimri the Nasi. He asks what is happening in these weeks that tzaddikim fall.

title.en: The meraglim and the Nephilim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the meraglim lost their bitachon when they saw the Nephilim, and identifies the Nephilim of Bereishis as angels who opposed the creation of man, were cast down to earth and brought on the Mabul. He then gives a rule: the Torah is not a history book but repeats itself in every generation and person, so we too meet Nephilim in these forty days.

title.en: Place, time and soul

summary.en: Citing Sefer Yetzirah, the Mashgiach explains that whatever exists in place is found in time and in the soul: the Kodesh HaKodashim in place, Yom Kippur in time and the Kohen Gadol among souls, all meeting on Yom Kippur. Therefore, if there are fallen souls, Nephilim, there are also fallen times.

title.en: The Three Weeks: great days that fell

summary.en: Turning to the Three Weeks, which begin that night, the Mashgiach describes their mourning and asks whether they are really small days. He answers that they are great days which have fallen, destined according to the Navi Zechariah to become the most joyous days when Moshiach comes, and that their fall is felt in the heaviness people find in learning and davening.

title.en: Lifting the days: dig for the treasure

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what to do about the heaviness: not to be pulled down like the generation of the Mabul, but like Noach, Yehoshua and Kalev to strengthen emunah, learning and tefillah and lift the days. He explains Moshe's word 'dig' to the meraglim with the Rama MiPano's reading of 'bikurei anavim': these are days of the Satan, yet one who digs finds the good hidden in them.

title.en: Proofs that these are great days

summary.en: The Mashgiach proves the greatness of these days: Aharon's 'chag laHashem machar' pointed to Shiva Asar B'Tammuz, and the Chasam Sofer calculates that Rus conceived Oved on that day, so the Three Weeks begin with Moshiach and end with him, born on Tisha B'Av according to the Midrash. He adds a remez: 'somech Hashem lechol hanoflim' equals Tammuz in gematria, while Av, which is only bent, matches 'zokef lechol hakefufim'.

title.en: Pinchas and the mission of the Three Weeks

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Parshas Pinchas, read in the weeks of churban, speaks of dividing Eretz Yisrael and lists the korbanos of all the Yamim Tovim, because these days are destined to be holidays, and brings the Chozeh of Lublin that the three Shabbosos of the Three Weeks hold Pesach, Shavuos and Sukkos. The mission is to transform these weeks, as Hashem turned Bilaam's curse into a blessing out of love.

title.en: Lavan, Bilaam, Naval and Barzilai

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from Targum Yonasan that Bilaam was Lavan, and from the Arizal that this soul passed through Bilaam and Naval until it became Barzilai HaGiladi, who did the opposite of Naval for Dovid HaMelech. He asks why so wicked a soul was transformed so fast, and answers that Lavan had good at his core: his children Rachel, Leah, Zilpah and Bilhah and his son-in-law Yaakov, whose initials spell Barzilai.

title.en: Balak's hidden good and the season of transformation

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that even Balak had good within him, since Eglon, father of Rus and ancestor of Dovid HaMelech and Moshiach, came from him. From here he calls this the season of transformation: whoever suspects something bad in himself should turn it to good, for the people of these parshiyos were great people who fell and must get up; then he asks why Kalev and Yehoshua did not fall.

title.en: The kernel of chametz: the missing tefillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a tzaddik who prepared a perfect Pesach yet found a kernel of wheat in his soup at the Seder; an angel told him in a dream that he had forgotten to daven for a kosher Pesach, and that a bird had dropped the kernel down the chimney. So too Yehoshua was saved by Moshe's tefillah and Kalev by davening at the graves of the Avos, and the Mashgiach closes with a tefillah that the Three Weeks be transformed into sasson and simcha.

catalogTitle: צורך המיוחד להדגיש אמיתיות התורה לדורנו

oneLiner.en: In a time of hester panim, when open miracles are not seen, the Mashgiach shows why the truth of the Torah rests on events an entire people witnessed: Matan Torah before millions, and a sefer Torah that described what that whole generation had seen with its own eyes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by describing the present as a time of hester panim, when the open miracles of earlier tzaddikim are no longer seen. After a long stretch of unusable audio, he brings the passuk in Devarim that asks whether any nation ever heard the voice of G-d speaking as the Jews did, and stresses that at Matan Torah the whole people, millions of men, women and children, became prophets at once; an event witnessed by so many cannot be denied. He then turns to the last mitzvah of the Torah, that every Jew write a sefer Torah. All the sifrei Torah were identical, and the generation that received them, who had been children under twenty in the wilderness, found in it the events of the forty years they had lived through, and agreed that it was true. In the last part, he cites the principle that the Torah will never be exchanged, and argues that a Torah of hard obligations would not have been accepted had it not been true.

en: The Mashgiach describes the present as a time of hester panim, when the open miracles of earlier generations are not seen.
At Matan Torah an entire people of millions heard Hashem speak and became prophets, something no other nation ever claimed.
An event that happened before so many people and was handed down through the generations cannot be denied.
Every Jew was commanded to write his own sefer Torah, and all the sifrei Torah were exactly the same.
The generation that received the sefer Torah had lived through the forty years it described and confirmed that it was true.
The Mashgiach cites the principle of faith that the Torah will never be exchanged for another.

catalogTitle: בהירות האמונה ע”י השבע פלאים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that Jewish history, read like the Megillah, reveals Hashem's hand, and he presents the 'seven wonders' of Jewish history as a way to clarify emunah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that strengthening oneself in the fundamentals of emunah requires basic knowledge, and that Hashem is seen in daily events just as in the Megillah, where every simple detail turns out to be part of the miracle; this is why the Megillah is read a second time. Jewish history is such a Megillah, as Moshe Rabbeinu says in Haazinu, 'remember the days of old'. He recalls that no other nation ever claimed a revelation to an entire people. He then describes the 'seven wonders of history' taught in Aish HaTorah courses: the eternal people, the spread of belief in one G-d, the bond to Eretz Yisrael, the return to Torah, the refusal to assimilate, the foretold hatred, and the small people that survives. He adds the Septuagint as proof the Torah text was not altered, and closes with the Torah's promises that the Jewish people will remain forever.

en: Like the Megillah, where every ordinary event turns out to be part of the miracle, all of Jewish history shows Hashem's hand once one looks back at it.
Moshe Rabbeinu told the Jews to remember the days of old and reflect on every generation, and they would see that all of history is for the sake of Bnei Yisrael.
No other nation has ever had, or even claimed, a revelation of Hashem to an entire people.
The seven wonders are each a wonder in itself, and looked at together they are all connected to one another.
The first wonder is that the Jews are an eternal people, while the great empires that ruled over them, Egypt, Bavel, Greece and Rome, have vanished.
The Septuagint, translated at the start of the second Beis Hamikdash, shows that nothing was added to the Torah later.
The Torah promises many times that the Jewish people will remain an eternal people, small in number but never destroyed.

title.en: Seeing Hashem in events, as in the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that to strengthen oneself in emunah one needs foundational knowledge, and that Hashem is seen in daily events. He explains that in the Megillah each ordinary event is part of the miracle, which is why it is read a second time, by day.

title.en: Jewish history as a Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Jewish history a Megillah and brings Moshe Rabbeinu's words in Haazinu to remember the days of old and see that all history is for Bnei Yisrael. He recalls that no other nation ever had a revelation of Hashem to a whole people.

title.en: Wonders no nation has seen; the Aish HaTorah courses

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk from the week's parsha that Hashem will do wonders before the whole people, and describes the Aish HaTorah courses in Jerusalem that bring young people to teshuvah by showing them the wonders of Jewish history. He introduces their series on the 'seven wonders of history'.

title.en: The eternal people; teaching the world one G-d

summary.en: The first wonder: the Jews are an eternal people while Egypt, Bavel, Greece and Rome have disappeared. The second: the Jews brought the world to believe in one G-d, so that Christians and Muslims build on the Torah.

title.en: Wonders three through seven

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the remaining wonders: the bond to Eretz Yisrael after two thousand years, the return to Torah after the 'isms', the refusal to assimilate, the foretold hatred of the nations, and the small people that survives, illustrated by the numbers of Yishmael's and Yitzchak's descendants.

title.en: Where to begin: the eternity promised in the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says each wonder needs long explanation, and that the first thing to learn is that the Jews are an eternal people, as the Torah foretold. He recalls that the whole Torah was given before all of Israel, who remembered the miracles of forty years and passed them on, so it could not have been invented later.

title.en: The Septuagint as proof

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how King Talmai had the elders translate the Torah into Greek in separate rooms, and all made the same changes, as the Gemara in Megillah relates. Since this translation from early in the second Beis Hamikdash still exists, no one can claim something was inserted into the Torah later.

title.en: The Torah's promise that Israel will remain

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds that the mesorah from generation to generation cannot be falsified, and brings pesukim from Malachi, Bechukosai and Yeshayahu that the Jewish people will remain forever, small in number but eternal.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows three wonders of the Jewish people: their eternity, the nations' jealous hatred of the chosen people who light up the world, and their unique bond with Eretz Yisroel, which blooms only for them.

abstract.en: Continuing from the previous week, the Mashgiach recalls that the mighty empires that destroyed the Beis Hamikdash have vanished while the small Jewish people lives on, as the pesukim in Malachi, the tochachah, Nitzavim and Yeshayahu promise. He then asks why the nations are so bothered that Jews call themselves the chosen people, and answers that they know it is true; their jealousy turns into hatred, as the Zohar shows from Yosef and his brothers. He reads Mark Twain and Tolstoy on the Jew's immortality and a letter of President Adams on the Jews as the teachers of belief in one G-d, and adds the Abarbanel and Spain's decline after the expulsion. The third wonder is the bond with Eretz Yisroel: Jews still mourn it after two thousand years, and the land, desolate under every other people, now blooms as the Jews return, which the Gemara calls the clearest sign of the end of exile.

en: The great empires that oppressed Israel have vanished, while the small Jewish people has outlived them all, as Hashem promised through the Torah and the Neviim.
The nations hate the Jews because they are jealous of them, and they are jealous because they know the Jews really are the chosen people.
Honest non-Jewish thinkers such as Mark Twain, Tolstoy and President Adams admitted the Jew's eternity and his role in bringing belief in G-d to the world.
The Jews are a light to the nations, bringing wisdom and emunah to the whole world, as Yeshayahu foretold.
No other people longs for a land it left so long ago; the Jews still mourn Eretz Yisroel after two thousand years of exile.
Eretz Yisroel is fruitful only when the Jews are there; under others it stayed desolate, and its blooming today is the Gemara's clearest sign of the end of exile.

title.en: The eternal people outlives the empires

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls last week's theme, that the empires who destroyed the Beis Hamikdash vanished while Israel lives on, and brings the promises of Malachi, the tochachah, Nitzavim and Yeshayahu that the Jews will remain a small but enduring people and return to their land.

title.en: Why the nations hate the chosen people

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why it bothers the nations that Jews call themselves chosen, when other peoples' boasts are only laughed at. He answers that they know it is true and cannot become Jews themselves, so they are jealous, and jealousy breeds hatred, as the Zohar learns from Yosef and his brothers; this is the root of the persecutions throughout the exile.

title.en: Mark Twain and Tolstoy on the eternal Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads, in English, Mark Twain's description of the Jew who is barely one percent of mankind yet outlived Egypt, Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome, and Tolstoy's words that the Jew is the emblem of eternity whom no persecution could destroy. He concludes with Moshe Rabbeinu's words that the nations will call Israel a wise and understanding people.

title.en: Surviving every catastrophe; the Abarbanel and Spain

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the catastrophes since those writers, the pogroms, the Holocaust and the wars, which the Jews survived as the eternal people and a light to the nations. Every king had Jewish advisors; the Abarbanel, minister of the king of Spain, refused to stay when the Jews were expelled, and Spain sank into insignificance without its Jews.

title.en: A light to the nations: President Adams's letter

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Christianity and Islam both come from the Jews, who brought emunah to the world, as Yeshayahu said that nations will walk by Israel's light. He reads a letter of President John Adams answering a call to make Jews second-class citizens, that the Hebrews did more to civilize mankind than any nation by teaching belief in one supreme G-d, and notes that Jews still fill the highest offices, fulfilling the blessing to Avraham.

title.en: The third wonder: longing for Eretz Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach moves to the third wonder, the bond of the Jews with Eretz Yisroel: no other people longs for a homeland it lost, yet Jews mention and mourn it three times a day. He tells of Napoleon finding Jews mourning on Tisha B'Av and saying such a people will surely return to its land, and adds that whole communities gave their lives for Hashem, which no other nation can claim.

title.en: A land that blooms only for the Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Torah's praise of the good land the Jews were brought to, and the tochachah's warning that in exile it would become desolate, so that a stranger would see it burnt and unsown. He concludes that with the Jews the land is the most fruitful, and without them a wasteland, as he himself saw on his first visit some thirty years earlier.

title.en: The blooming land as the revealed end

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the land, which for two thousand years no nation could settle, is now covered with fields and forests as the Jews return, and brings the Gemara in Sanhedrin that there is no clearer sign of the end than Eretz Yisroel giving its fruit. He recalls the tiny fruits once brought from there and its poverty, contrasts them with today's prosperity, and calls it a wonder before one's eyes.

catalogTitle: The Hidden חסד of the חורבן

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chodesh Av carries the mercy of a Father, since the Churban fell on wood and stone to save Klal Yisrael, and he shows why Esav's showy kibud av outdoes Yaakov's and lets him prevail in Av.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Chodesh Av, a month of mourning that will be turned to joy, and with the Maharal: the curses run backwards, from vav to hey, so they are only temporary. He links Tammuz and Av to Reuven and Shimon. Then he brings Avimi, who honored his father perfectly and was helped to explain why the psalm of the Churban is called a song: Hashem poured His anger on wood and stone and saved the people. Kibud av awakens the mercy of the Father above, and the name Av itself means that Hashem punishes as a father. The Mashgiach then asks why Esav outdid Yaakov in kibud av and so prevails in Av. Esav's honor is external, a veneer driven by the Satan, like the goy of Ashkelon who did not know his true father. Kibud av and love of Eretz Yisrael share one root, and together with tzedakah they build the Beis HaMikdash.

en: The curses of Bechukosai run from vav to hey, against the order of the alphabet, which shows, as the Maharal explains, that they are a passing state that will turn into blessing.
The Churban was an act of a Father's mercy: Hashem poured His anger on the wood and stones of the Beis HaMikdash so that Klal Yisrael would survive, which is why Asaf calls the psalm a song.
Honoring parents awakens above the conduct of Hashem as our Father, who has mercy on His children.
The name of the month, Av, tells that Hashem punishes like a father, with mercy and to set the son straight, so Av is a month of consolation.
Esav's kibud av surpasses Yaakov's only on the outside; inwardly he wished his father dead, and the Mashgiach says the Satan drives the nations' devotion to this mitzvah.
Kibud av and the longing for Eretz Yisrael share one root, since both come from a person's origin, and kibud av and tzedakah are the two mitzvos that build the Beis HaMikdash.

candidateTopics: Eretz Yisrael as a Jew's origin
tzedakah and the rebuilding of the Beis HaMikdash

title.en: Av, and curses that run backwards

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the coming of Chodesh Av, an unwelcome month of mourning, and the hope that its fast will become a day of joy. He brings the Midrash that the blessings run from aleph to tav while the curses run backwards from vav to hey, and the Maharal's explanation that the curses are outside Hashem's plan and only temporary.

title.en: Tammuz is Reuven, Av is Shimon

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that Reuven, fourth in the camps and among the nesi'im, corresponds to Tammuz, which is why the three weeks begin around Korach and Dasan and Aviram. Shimon, fifth, corresponds to Av, and in Pinchas we read of Zimri, the nasi of Shimon.

title.en: Avimi and the song of Asaf

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara about Avimi, who stood bent over his sleeping father holding water, and in that merit explained why Asaf calls his psalm on the Churban a song and not a lament. Hashem transferred the punishment from Klal Yisrael to the wood and stones of the Beis HaMikdash, and the people were saved.

title.en: Kibud av awakens the Father above

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every mitzvah awakens something corresponding above, and honoring parents switches on Hashem's conduct as a merciful Father. He asks why, then, Hashem seems not to act as a Father in a long golus, and answers from Avimi: the Churban itself came from a Father's mercy.

title.en: The name Av and the comfort it brings

summary.en: Following the Maharal's rule that a name reveals one's mission, the Mashgiach shows that Avimi spells 'days of Av' and his father Avuha holds hey before vav, the curses in reverse. Av means Hashem punishes as a father, so one weeps but not too much, and the month will become one of joy.

title.en: Esav's kibud av and his hold on Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the nations seem more devoted to kibud av than Jews, and that Yaakov feared Esav for his kibud av and his living in Eretz Yisrael. Av, the month of the Father, is Esav's month of success, when he destroyed the Beis HaMikdash twice; yet Esav's honor was external, since he hoped for his father's death in order to kill Yaakov.

title.en: The Satan behind the goy's kibud av

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a great rav in Poland who as a child told his father that the same Satan that sends the goyish boys to school keeps him in bed, and suggests the Satan drives Esav's excellence in kibud av. He brings the Gemara of Dama ben Nesina and the Chida that Hashem is a King to the nations but a Father only to Yidden.

title.en: Fine clothes and third-person speech

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who said Esav outdid him by serving his father in special garments, and the Ksav Sofer, who notes that Esav spoke to Yitzchak in the third person like a subject to a king while Yaakov spoke simply. A son at home needs no veneer because of the love between them; Esav shows off his kibud av like the chazir shows its split hooves.

title.en: Why both examples come from Ashkelon

summary.en: The Mashgiach argues that a loving Jewish father would be upset had his son lost a fortune rather than wake him, so Dama ben Nesina's conduct reflects a king and subject, not intimacy. He asks why the Gemara names Ashkelon, and explains that the Pelishtim there descended from swapped wives and lacked the natural bond to a father, so their kibud av is only external.

title.en: Kibud av and Eretz Yisrael share one root

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one honors parents because they are one's origin, and a Jew longs for Eretz Yisrael because Adam was formed from its earth, from the place of the Beis HaMikdash and the mizbeiach. So the reward of kibud av is long days in the land. He brings the Maharal that the nations honor parents more because their whole world is the body their parents gave them, while a Jew's neshamah existed before.

title.en: What the Gemara's question really asks

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how a goy of Ashkelon could teach the measure of kibud av, and rereads the Gemara: it asks how great this mitzvah is, and answers that the Satan drives the goyim to it because kibud av holds the building of the Beis HaMikdash and the end of golus. He compares tzedakah, which also builds the Beis HaMikdash, citing the Gemara on not taking tzedakah from a goy and Daniel's punishment for advising Nevuchadnetzar to give tzedakah.

title.en: The Torah as Father; welcoming Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach extends kibud av to a teacher and to the Torah itself, which one should learn with respect as Hashem's Torah. He closes that Av is welcomed with bitachon and emunah, that Zimri will also have his tikkun, and that Tammuz and Menachem Av equal Melech HaMashiach in gematria.

catalogTitle: עריכות הפליאות יחד שייך דוקה ע”י הקב”ה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that the Torah foretold Jewish history, the return of baalei teshuvah, exile, a small and hated nation that survives, and that these wonders contradict one another so that only Hashem could have put them together.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues his series on the wonders of Jewish history. Jews always kept the Torah; the idol worship found in Tanach was a powerful yetzer hara, like today's trials, not a departure from the Torah. That departure began about two hundred years ago with the Haskalah in Germany, whose destruction the Meshech Chochmah foresaw. Now, unexpectedly, a movement of baalei teshuvah has begun, a drizzle before the storm of teshuvah that will come with Moshiach, as the Torah and the prophets foretold, together with the flowering of Eretz Yisrael. He then reviews the prophecies of exile, of the Jews remaining few, and of the hatred of the nations. His central point is that these wonders contradict each other: a scattered, tiny, hated people should not survive, yet the Torah says it is eternal and a light to the nations. No human mind could foresee such a combination; only the Creator, who leads history, could.

en: The idol worship recorded in Tanach was a strong yetzer hara that people stumbled in, not an abandonment of the Torah, which began only with the Haskalah about two hundred years ago.
The rise of baalei teshuvah, unforeseen even a generation ago, fulfills the Torah's and the prophets' words that before Moshiach Jews will return and hunger to hear the word of Hashem.
The Torah foretold the exile, that the Jews would remain few among the nations, and that they would be an object of scorn among them.
These prophecies contradict one another and reason, so no historian could have predicted them together; only Hashem could foretell them.
A people scattered, tiny and hated should have disappeared like mighty Bavel, Persia, Greece and Rome, yet the Jews remain a people and even a light to the nations.

candidateTopics: Jewish history as proof of the Torah

title.en: Jews kept the Torah until the Haskalah

summary.en: Returning to the wonders of Jewish history, the Mashgiach explains that the idol worship in Tanach was a strong yetzer hara, abolished by the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, comparable to today's trials of immorality and the internet, and not a departure from the Torah. That departure began only about two hundred years ago in Germany with the Haskalah and the Reform and Conservative movements.

title.en: From Haskalah to the baal teshuvah movement

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites the Meshech Chochmah, who wrote that the Haskalah began in Germany and that destruction would begin there too, then mentions Zionism and communism. Then, some twenty or thirty years ago, a new phenomenon of baalei teshuvah began, which R' Shlomke of Zvhil foresaw; the Mashgiach notes the Lubavitcher Rebbe's strengthening of it and the fire of baalei teshuvah today.

title.en: Signs before Moshiach foretold in the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares today's teshuvah to the drizzle that precedes a storm, and ties it to the signs of Moshiach: the fruits of Eretz Yisrael that now go out to the whole world, the prophet Amos's hunger to hear the word of Hashem, and the Torah's promise in Nitzavim that Jews will return. He concludes that such foreknowledge shows the truth of the Torah.

title.en: The prophecy of exile and a remnant

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Moshe Rabbeinu's prophecy, as the Jews are about to enter Eretz Yisrael, that they will sin and be exiled, noting that the Greek translation of the Torah shows it was written long before. He cites the pesukim in Bechukosai and Va'eschanan that they will be scattered and remain few, yet will survive because Hashem leads them there, unlike the vanished great empires.

title.en: The wonder of the nations' hatred

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the hatred of the nations toward Jews, seen most starkly in the cruelty of the Germans under Hitler, and shows that the Torah foretold in Ki Savo that Israel would be an object of scorn among the nations. He repeats that the Torah also promised the Jews would remain few in number.

title.en: The wonders contradict each other

summary.en: Having gone through the wonders, the Mashgiach states the main point: they contradict one another, so reason could never connect them, and only the Ribono shel Olam could write them through Moshe and the prophets. Jewish history is unique, with no precedent a historian could extrapolate from; he frames this as one fact, A, contradicting another, B.

title.en: Eternal, scattered and hated: how can it be?

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the contradiction: no nation suffered such slaughter, and whole communities chose death over conversion, yet the Torah says the scattered few are an eternal people. He explains the hatred, citing Rashi's 'Esav hates Yaakov' and Haman's complaint that their laws differ, as the dislike of the unlike, and shows from the German Jews and Hitler that assimilation only increased it.

title.en: A light to the nations, and only the Creator foretold it

summary.en: The Mashgiach sums up the contradictions and adds another: the small, hated, landless people is a light to the nations, prominent far beyond its numbers. He recalls the fruitfulness of Eretz Yisrael and tells how Ben Gurion agreed to fund yeshivos expecting them to fade, while they grew stronger. He concludes that only the Ribono shel Olam, who created and leads all, could foretell this history.

catalogTitle: הקדמה; ביאור קושיא הראשונה שבספר; ביאור כחו של שבועה.

oneLiner.en: Opening a series on Tanya, the Mashgiach introduces the sefer and its author, raises the first question of chapter one about the oath to be a tzaddik yet see oneself as a rasha, and explains why a soul is put under oath before it comes down to the world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Ba'al HaTanya, a disciple of the Maggid who excelled in the wisdom of Torah, and explains that Tanya, unlike sefarim of derashos on the parsha, sets out the foundations of Chassidus in an ordered sequence. Tanya, he stresses, belongs to all of Klal Yisrael, and he tells how Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz learned it with his talmidim. Through the title page and the passuk 'ki karov', he shows that yiras Shamayim is near only by the long road. He explains the opening word 'Tanya' as breaking a klipah and as letters of the future tense, a sign of teshuvah. He then sets out the first question: the oath to be a tzaddik while seeing oneself as a rasha clashes with serving Hashem in simcha. Finally, from Avraham's oath to Eliezer, he explains that an oath releases hidden reserves of strength, and links the oath of the soul to the strength of Shabbos.

en: Tanya sets out the foundations of the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Maggid as one ordered sequence from beginning to end, not as derashos tied to the pesukim of the parsha.
The Mashgiach stresses that Tanya is the sefer of all of Klal Yisrael, learned throughout Poland and Hungary, and not the possession of one circle of Chassidim.
Yiras Shamayim is 'near' only by way of the long road; there are no shortcuts to it.
The first question of the sefer is how the oath to see oneself as a rasha fits with the need to serve Hashem in simcha.
An oath draws on a person's hidden reserves, strengths he does not know he has, for a time of emergency.
A shevuah carries the power of the seven days of creation and brings satiation and flow of blessing, which the soul needs to face the hard world.

title.en: The Ba'al HaTanya and the order of his sefer

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the Ba'al HaTanya as a disciple of the Maggid, greatest among them in the wisdom of Torah, and contrasts Tanya's ordered sequence with sefarim of derashos on the parsha. He notes the Ba'al HaTanya's emphasis on hisbonenus and chochmah, binah, da'as, and closes that 'these and those are the words of the living G-d'.

title.en: A sefer for all of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach says it is a great mistake to think Tanya belongs to one circle; it was learned across Poland and Hungary. He tells that Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz learned it with his talmidim, explains how he will present ideas from many sefarim, and describes how the Ba'al HaTanya printed the sefer because of copying errors, gathering it from sefarim and sofrim.

title.en: 'Ki karov': the long road to yiras Shamayim

summary.en: On the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar', the Mashgiach notes that yiras Shamayim is in fact very hard, as Shlomo HaMelech and the Mesillas Yesharim show. Through the Gemara's story of the short-and-long road and the long-and-short road, he explains that it is near only by the long way. He then turns to the name 'Sefer shel Beinonim'.

title.en: What learning Tanya can give

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells his listeners that the sefer can change their avodas Hashem and open the gates to other sefarim. He explains that all of Torah, including maaseh bereishis and maaseh merkavah, was given at Sinai, that only a small part of the Oral Torah remains, and that the Ba'al Shem Tov's talmidim used points of Kabbalah only where they bear on avodah, as Tanya will on a surface level.

title.en: Why the sefer opens with 'Tanya'

summary.en: The Mashgiach outlines chapter one as a chapter of questions, followed by introductory chapters before practical avodah. He discusses the Gemara in Niddah that opens with 'Tanya', brings the Zohar that a klipah bearing that name is broken by learning that begins with this word, and explains that its four letters are the letters of the future tense, as in 'Ehyeh', a sign of teshuvah.

title.en: The oath: a tzaddik who sees himself as a rasha

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the oath given to the soul, 'be a tzaddik and not a rasha, and even if the whole world calls you a tzaddik be in your eyes like a rasha', and asks how this fits with serving Hashem in simcha, which is the purpose of avodah. He shows the tension from both sides: seeing oneself as a rasha all one's life brings sadness, yet never feeling bad can lead to lightheadedness.

title.en: Why Avraham made Eliezer swear

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Avraham needed to make the faithful Eliezer swear, and likewise Yaakov with Yosef. He explains that people carry hidden strengths that emerge only in an emergency, and that Avraham knew Eliezer would face Lavan, identified with Bilaam, the head of the sitra achra. The oath would let Eliezer draw on reserves he could not otherwise reach.

title.en: What a shevuah is

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a shevuah is a great power: a person contains the whole creation, and a shevuah carries the strength of the seven days of creation. He derives the word from 'sova', satiation, and from 'shefa', since beis and peh interchange, and describes the world the soul enters as a hard place full of dangers, like a 'hall of horrors'.

title.en: The soul's oath and the strength of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that the soul, coming down from among the angels to a world of friction, needs the oath as Eliezer and Yosef did. He brings a teaching of the Slonimer tzaddikim comparing Shabbos to a warm inn for a traveler in the cold rain, and explains that the oath, like Shabbos, recharges the soul for its journey in this world.

catalogTitle: ביאור ענין מזל' האדם נברא תחת מזל - אבל לא צדיק או רשע. קושיא של איוב' בראת צדיקים בראת רשעים. ביאור מה זה צדיק.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that mazal decides a person's physical traits but not whether he is a tzaddik or a rasha, and uses this to explain Iyov's words and the Tanya's definition of a tzaddik as one who has no yetzer hara at all.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara's categories of tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo and the Ra'aya Mehemna's reading of them, then the Gemara in Berachos that the yetzer tov 'judges' the tzaddik, and Rabbah's claim to be a beinoni. He asks how Iyov could say that Hashem created tzaddikim and reshaim, when the angel announces at conception whether a person will be rich or poor, wise or foolish, but not whether he will be a tzaddik or a rasha. At length he explains what mazal is: the star and angel over each month, hour and moment of birth, and the place of birth, from which a person's physical traits flow down. Since Rabbah never sinned, a beinoni must be one who never sins; the Rosh Hashanah 'tzaddik' is a borrowed name. A true tzaddik has no yetzer hara, like Dovid HaMelech. Some are born so, and of these rare individuals Iyov spoke.

en: The angel at conception announces a person's physical lot (rich or poor, wise or foolish, strong or weak) but not whether he will be a tzaddik or a rasha, since that is left to his free choice.
Mazal is the star and its angel over the month, hour and moment of birth, and even the country of birth shapes a person; his physical bounty flows down to him through it.
Because Rabbah never sinned and was truthful, his calling himself a beinoni shows that a beinoni is one who never commits a sin.
The 'tzaddik' of the Rosh Hashanah judgment, one with more merits than sins, is only a borrowed name, meaning one who is found right in that judgment.
A true tzaddik has no yetzer hara at all, as Dovid HaMelech said that his heart was 'chalal', empty of it.
Some tzaddikim are born without a yetzer hara and some, like Dovid HaMelech, worked until they lost it; Iyov's words refer to the first kind, who are rare individuals.

title.en: Tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's categories of tzaddik v'tov lo, tzaddik v'ra lo and their counterparts. He contrasts the plain reading (a tzaddik who fares well or badly) with the Ra'aya Mehemna's reading, that tzaddik v'ra lo is a tzaddik who has evil within him but rules over it like a master over a dog on a leash.

title.en: Rabbah the beinoni and Iyov's question

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara at the end of Berachos that the yetzer tov is the tzaddik's judge, and Rabbah's statement that he is a beinoni. He then asks how Iyov could say Hashem created tzaddikim and reshaim, when the angel at conception announces a person's physical traits but not whether he will be a tzaddik or a rasha, so as not to compel his choice.

title.en: Mazal: the stars of the months

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every person has a mazal, a star in the heavens in which an angel is clothed. Each month has its own permutation of the Name Havaya and its own mazal, which is why Cheshvan brings withering and Kislev a new light, and a person born in a month carries its traits.

title.en: Hour, place and the meaning of 'mazal'

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds that every hour and moment has its mazal, and that the country of birth also shapes a person, while Eretz Yisroel is above mazal. He explains that 'mazal' means flowing down, like 'nozlim', and that 'gad' also means mazal, and concludes that the angel announces everything by mazal except tzaddik and rasha.

title.en: A beinoni never sins

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what a beinoni is, given that Rabbah never stopped learning and was a man of truth. He goes through the Tanya's definitions of a rasha, including one who could learn and does not, and concludes that since Rabbah had not even bitul Torah, a beinoni must be one who never sins.

title.en: The Rosh Hashanah tzaddik is a borrowed name

summary.en: If a beinoni never sins, the Mashgiach asks, what is a tzaddik, and how does this fit the Gemara in Rosh Hashanah where a tzaddik is one with more merits than sins? He answers that there 'tzaddik' is a borrowed name, like a litigant who wins his din Torah: he is right in that judgment, not a tzaddik in truth.

title.en: Dovid HaMelech's empty heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Dovid HaMelech's words 'v'libi chalal b'kirbi': chalal means empty, so the left chamber of his heart had no yetzer hara, and it also means killed, since he slew it through fasting. A tzaddik is one with no yetzer hara, and such tzaddikim are few, as the Gemara says Hashem planted them in every generation.

title.en: Tzaddikim who are born complete

summary.en: The Mashgiach sets out the Tanya's premise: a tzaddik has no yetzer hara, either from birth or by working until he lost it, while a beinoni has two judges and chooses between them. Tzaddikim born complete come down for the sake of others, and since they have no choice they may remember earlier gilgulim, as the Yismach Moshe remembered being a sheep of Yaakov Avinu.

title.en: Iyov's answer: rare individuals

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Iyov spoke of tzaddikim created complete, and of reshaim born to be wicked, whom Hashem also needs for His plan for creation. Dovid HaMelech instead had to repair Adam's flaw and work until he became a tzaddik; most people are neither, and have the choice to be at least a beinoni.

catalogTitle: Understanding the מועד of 'ט באב and the יו”ט of ט”ו באב

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Tisha B'Av is truly a mo'ed rooted in Pesach, Shabbos and Shemini Atzeres, destined to become a Yom Tov, and that Tu B'Av is the Yom Tov of the ba'al teshuvah who rises from the grave.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Mishnah's term 'the week in which Tisha B'Av falls' and asks why Shabbos, the day of blessing, ushers in the aveilus, and why Tisha B'Av is called a mo'ed on which Tachanun is not said. He shows that Pesach fixes the weekday of Tisha B'Av and that the beitzah on the Seder plate plants it, because there is no absolute destruction for Klal Yisrael: Tisha B'Av is rooted in geulah, Moshiach is born on it, and every aveilus, even a private one, draws its laws from Yom Tov. He explains why Shabbos Chazon is the greatest Shabbos and why the meal before Tisha B'Av on Shabbos is like Shlomo's feast, through the Arizal's teaching that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, whose day is Shemini Atzeres. Through the three dimensions of place, time and soul he explains the mo'ed of Tisha B'Av, and he ends with the Jew lying in his grave, whose Yom Tov is Tu B'Av, the day of the ba'al teshuvah.

en: The aveilus of Tisha B'Av week begins only from the Shabbos before it, so Shabbos, the day of blessing, is what ushers in the aveilus.
Tisha B'Av is a mo'ed, a time of meeting with Hashem, which is why Tachanun is not said on it.
The first day of Pesach fixes the weekday of Tisha B'Av because Tisha B'Av is rooted in the day of geulah and is destined to become a Yom Tov.
There is no absolute destruction or absolute evil for Klal Yisrael; every aveilus is only a veil over something good, as the law of seven days of mourning is learned from the Yom Tov.
Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, so Tisha B'Av is in a sense a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres, Shlomo's day, and will turn back into it.
Every mo'ed carries a blessing to take home; the blessing of Tisha B'Av is the knowledge that Hashem is with Klal Yisrael even in churban.
Tu B'Av is the Yom Tov of the ba'al teshuvah who leaves his grave, and so it is greater than Pesach, Shavuos and Sukkos.

title.en: Why Shabbos ushers in the aveilus

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the laws of the week of Tisha B'Av depend on the Shabbos before it, and asks why the Shabbos of blessing should usher in aveilus. He then asks why Tisha B'Av is called a mo'ed, a meeting, so that Tachanun is not said on it.

title.en: Pesach sets the day of Tisha B'Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Pesach and Tisha B'Av as two extremes, and shows that Pesach, the head of the festivals, fixes the weekday of Tisha B'Av. He answers that Tisha B'Av is rooted in the day of geulah, is destined to become a day of simcha, and is the day Moshiach is born.

title.en: The beitzah and a passing churban

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the beitzah on the Seder plate plants Tisha B'Av in Pesach and is the remedy for Amalek, who brought about Tisha B'Av. Tisha B'Av is a passing condition, and Pesach gives it the first place among the Yamim Tovim.

title.en: Shabbos and the bittersweet aveilus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the week is Hashem's own calendar and its special day is Shabbos, so no aveilus can begin without Shabbos; the aveilus of Tisha B'Av is full of nechamah and hope. He brings the Gemara deriving seven days of mourning from Yom Tov to show that even a private aveilus is only a veil.

title.en: Shabbos Chazon, the greatest Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Shabbos Chazon is called the greatest Shabbos of the year, and that its haftarah is from Yeshayahu, the navi of geulah, not Yirmiyahu, the navi of churban. He suggests that 'Chazon' points to the heart, which senses the geulah hidden under the aveilus.

title.en: Tefillin at Minchah and Shlomo's feast

summary.en: The Mashgiach suggests that tefillin are not worn on Tisha B'Av morning because we still hope it will become a Yom Tov. He then contrasts the poor seudah hamafsekes with the Gemara's rule that when Tisha B'Av follows Shabbos one eats a meal like Shlomo's feast in his time.

title.en: Yirmiyahu, gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Arizal's teaching that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, who returned to see the destruction of the Beis HaMikdash he built. Each tzaddik has his day: Tisha B'Av is Yirmiyahu's, Shemini Atzeres is Shlomo's, a sample of the days of Moshiach when the moon was full.

title.en: Tisha B'Av, a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that no person ever reached complete fulfillment except Shlomo HaMelech, a sample of the days of Moshiach. When Shlomo returned as Yirmiyahu his day became Tisha B'Av, so Tisha B'Av is a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres and will change back; this is why the meal before it on Shabbos is like Shlomo in his time.

title.en: Why Tu B'Av is the greatest Yom Tov

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah that there were no Yamim Tovim like Tu B'Av and Yom Kippur, and the Gemara's account of the generation of the desert dying every Tisha B'Av until the decree stopped. He asks why that should make Tu B'Av greater than Pesach, Shavuos and Sukkos.

title.en: Place, time and soul: the mo'ed

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Sefer Yetzirah's three dimensions of place, time and soul, which meet on Yom Kippur in the Kodesh HaKodashim through the Kohen Gadol. A mo'ed is a meeting with Hashem from which one takes home a blessing, and the blessing of Tisha B'Av is that Hashem sits with Klal Yisrael on the ground.

title.en: Souls that are Shabbos and Yom Tov

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that time is duplicated in soul: a talmid chacham is called Shabbos, and the one who supports him receives blessing from him as one receives from Shabbos. Lesser souls who work but are bound to Torah are Yom Tov, and others are a mo'ed.

title.en: The Tisha B'Av Jew and Tu B'Av

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the gifted Jew who could have been great but lies in his grave thinking it is life; he is a Tisha B'Av, yet we do not despair, since no Jew is lost forever. When he leaves the grave and does teshuvah, his Yom Tov is Tu B'Av, greater than all the festivals, as a ba'al teshuvah is greater than a tzaddik.

title.en: Dancing in the vineyards; the gold will shine

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the daughters of Yisrael dancing on Tu B'Av as those who came out of the grave, and calls on those still in it to join them. He compares the meal before Tisha B'Av on Shabbos to the Ran's explanation of the meal of Erev Yom Kippur, and closes with the hope that the tarnished gold will be polished and Tu B'Av will become the Yom Tov of the world.

catalogTitle: שתי נשמות לישראל' טעם שהטומאה נקרא קליפה' ד' קליפות וד' יסודות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's opening teaching that every Jew has two souls, why the side of evil is called sitra achra and klipah, and how the four klipos parallel the four elements.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins Tanya chapter one: every Jew, tzaddik or rasha, has two souls. The animal soul gives the biological life a person shares with every creature and comes from the earth; the G-dly soul comes from above and longs to cleave to Hashem. The animal soul comes from the sitra achra, 'the other side', and one cannot stand on both sides of the fence, as the Kotzker's vort about dancing at two weddings shows. It is also called klipah, a shell: it guards the fruit, but it must be broken to reach it, and breaking it is a person's purpose. The Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the king's seven walls and stories of Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev and Rabbi Aharon of Karlin show the sweetness waiting beyond. He then explains why the animal soul dwells in the blood, and the four klipos parallel to the four elements, illustrated by the layers of a walnut.

en: Every Jew, whether tzaddik or rasha, has two souls: an animal soul from the side of klipah and a G-dly soul that is a part of G-d above.
The animal soul is the life force a person shares with every living creature, and its seat is the blood.
The source of evil is called sitra achra, 'the other side', because one cannot be on both sides of the fence at once.
It is called klipah because, like a shell, it is needed only to guard the fruit, and because it must be broken through to reach the fruit; breaking it is a person's purpose in the world.
There are four klipos, parallel to the four elements that come from the four letters of Hashem's Name; the finest, klipas nogah, lets light through and can be turned to holiness.

four elements and the four-letter Name

title.en: Every Jew has two souls

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter one: every Jew, tzaddik or rasha, has two souls. He explains the animal soul that a person shares with every creature and the G-dly soul from above, mentions a third, intellectual soul that the Tanya does not discuss here, and describes what each of the two souls desires.

title.en: Sitra achra: you cannot dance at two weddings

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the animal soul comes from the sitra achra, Aramaic for 'the other side', and that one cannot stand on both sides of the fence. He brings a vort of the Kotzker about dancing at two weddings, notes that what people say has truth in it, and explains that 'eishes chayil' means either the Torah or a physical wife, but not both together.

title.en: Why evil is called klipah

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives two reasons for the name klipah: a shell only guards the fruit and is thrown away once the fruit is taken, and one must break through the shell to reach the fruit. He ties this to the keruvim and the flaming sword guarding Gan Eden and says breaking the klipah is a person's purpose.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of seven walls

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of a king surrounded by seven guarded walls: soldiers stop after the gifts of the first walls, but the prince breaks through all seven to reach his father, who then shows him the walls were only an illusion.

title.en: Wanting the King Himself

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the parable: a person must break the seven walls of the bad middos, and the one who serves Hashem out of love wants only Hashem Himself, as the Ba'al HaTanya would say in his dveikus. He brings the Gemara that the yetzer hara will look to tzaddikim like a mountain and to reshaim like a hair, and Dovid HaMelech's words that Torah is sweeter than honey.

title.en: The poritz's pleasures and a tzaddik's

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, about to light Chanukah candles, asked a man about the poritz's food and bed and concluded that the poritz is well off but he himself is better off, and how Rabbi Aharon of Karlin dismissed a poritz sledding on sugar in midsummer next to his own pleasure in Nishmas on Shabbos. Each person feels the sweetness according to how much klipah he has broken.

title.en: The animal soul dwells in the blood

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that holiness is likened to a nut whose shell must be cracked, then returns to the Tanya's text and its source in Rabbi Chaim Vital. He explains that the animal soul is clothed in the blood, as the passuk says, while the G-dly soul is in the brain, and gives a simple reason why the Torah forbids eating blood.

title.en: Four elements, four klipos, and the walnut

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the four elements come from the four letters of Hashem's Name, and that the four klipos parallel them. He brings Yechezkel's vision of the four barriers before the Kisei HaKavod, explains klipas nogah as a translucent curtain that lets light through and can be turned to holiness, and illustrates the four klipos with the four coverings of a walnut.

catalogTitle: ארבע קליפות הטמאות' ונוגה לו סביב' ארבע יסודות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's teaching that the animal soul of a Jew comes from kelipas nogah, which can be elevated to kedushah, and how all bad middos stem from its four elements: fire, water, air and earth.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the Tanya's opening: every Jew has an animal soul from the side of kelipah, and the four kelipos are the dross of the four letters of Hashem's Name. Three are wholly impure and must be destroyed; the fourth, kelipas nogah, can be transformed, as seen in milah and periah and in the four verbs of the brachah against the wicked. The animal soul of a Jew comes from nogah, so kosher food and natural middos can be raised to kedushah when used for serving Hashem, while a goy's animal soul comes from the three impure kelipos; this is the difference between tzedakah and mere charity. He then goes through the four elements: anger and pride from fire, desire and pleasure from water, frivolity, mockery, boasting and idle talk from air, laziness and sadness from earth, distinguishing sadness from constructive bitterness. He closes with the tree of knowledge of good and evil and the Midrash contrasting olos and shelamim.

en: The four kelipos are the dross of the four letters of Hashem's Name; three are wholly impure and must be broken, while the fourth, kelipas nogah, can be turned to kedushah.
The animal soul of a Jew comes from kelipas nogah, while that of a goy comes from the three impure kelipos.
Kosher food eaten for the sake of Heaven, with its strength used for Torah, tefilah and mitzvos, is elevated to kedushah, each according to his level.
All bad middos come from the four elements: anger and pride from fire, desires from water, frivolity, mockery, boasting and idle talk from air, laziness and sadness from earth.
Sadness is not a mitzvah and leads to sin, whereas bitterness over one's state stirs a person to act.
A goy can bring only an olah, which is wholly burned, while a Jew can bring a shelamim whose eating is part of the offering, because a Jew can eat for the sake of Heaven.

title.en: Review: the animal soul and the four kelipos

summary.en: After a request to keep up with the series on tape, the Mashgiach reviews the Tanya's words that every Jew has an animal soul from kelipah, from which all bad middos come, and that the four kelipos are the dross of the four letters of Hashem's Name, from which the four elements of all creation come.

title.en: Three impure kelipos and kelipas nogah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the first three kelipos are wholly impure and must be cut away, like the layers removed at milah, while nogah, like periah, is turned upward, and he finds the same four in the verbs of the brachah against the wicked in Nusach Ari. Forbidden food comes from the three, kosher food from nogah, and nogah is translucent; the four kelipos appear in Yechezkel's vision in chapter one.

title.en: A Jew's animal soul and elevating food

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the animal soul is the life force a person shares with all creatures, distinct from the breath of life Hashem blew into Adam. A Jew's animal soul comes from nogah and a goy's from the three impure kelipos, and with the example of a piece of kosher chicken he shows how the same food is dragged down or raised to kedushah depending on how it is eaten and used.

title.en: Natural middos: tzedakah versus charity

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that a person's natural middos, such as a love of giving, come from the animal soul; used for Heaven they are raised from nogah, used for evil they fall to the sitra achra. He distinguishes a Jew's tzedakah from a goy's charity, which is the animal kindness every creature has and is done for oneself, citing the Gemara that the kindness of the nations is a sin.

title.en: Fire: the source of anger and pride

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that all bad middos come from the four elements, beginning with anger and pride from fire. Every object holds all four elements, as burning wood shows, which he compares to modern science's matter and energy. Fire rises because its root is in the moon, which he says is why bedikas chametz is done at night.

title.en: Water and air: desire, frivolity, mockery

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that desire and pleasure come from water, the first element, linked to chesed and to the first of the seven voices; all pleasure and all life involve water, and water draws and attracts. From air come frivolity and mockery: wild music that releases a person from all restraint, and jokes, whose humor lies in their distance from reality.

title.en: Boasting, idle talk, and earth: sadness versus bitterness

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes boasting and idle talk as hollow air, with the picture of an honoree at a charity banquet. From earth come laziness and sadness, which leave a person lying idle; he contrasts sadness with bitterness that drives a person to act, brings a saying of Reb Aharon of Karlin, and shows from the Gemara and Rashi that sadness is never a mitzvah.

title.en: Good middos, the tree of knowledge, olah and shelamim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that even a Jew's inborn good middos, like mercy and kindness, come from the body and so from kelipas nogah, which holds good, as the secret of the tree of knowledge of good and evil. He brings the Midrash on 'awake, north, and come, south': the nations bring olos slaughtered in the north, Jews bring shelamim that are eaten, because only a Jew can eat for the sake of Heaven, apart from the few chasidei umos haolam who keep the seven mitzvos as the Rambam rules.

catalogTitle: שלש קליפות הטמאות אין להם תיקון עד ביאת המשיח. גוף ישראל מקליפת נוגה' ושל גוים משלש קליפות הטמאות - לפיכך חסד לאומים חטאת.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Tanya chapter one: the Jewish animal soul comes from klipas nogah, which can be elevated, while the nations' souls come from the three impure klipos, which have no tikkun until Moshiach, and therefore even the kindness of the nations is called a sin.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the rule that the three impure klipos cannot be elevated until Moshiach, while klipas nogah, the permitted pleasures, can. He asks how a forbidden mixture can then be nullified in sixty, and answers that such nullification is a glimmer of the days of Moshiach, as at the Exodus. He then reads the Tanya: even a Jew's animal soul is from nogah, while the nations' souls are from the impure klipos, so all the good they do is for themselves, even their mercy and charity. A Jew's mercy can become a mitzvah, shown in a story of a man who gave charity first from pity and then for the mitzvah. Through Yaakov's weeping at meeting Rachel, the Sukkah parable and the Maggid of Mezritch, he shows that a Jew's love and service are at root for Hashem. He closes with the Gemara on 'the kindness of nations is a sin' and explains chatas and zechus.

en: The three impure klipos have no tikkun until Moshiach, while klipas nogah, the permitted pleasures, can be elevated to holiness.
A Jew's animal soul comes from klipas nogah, while the vitalizing soul of the nations comes from the three impure klipos.
All the good the nations do, even out of mercy and charity, they do for themselves and not for Hashem.
A Jew's mercy, which comes from nogah, can be turned into the mitzvah of tzedakah and holiness.
Yaakov's love for Rachel was a love from holiness, not a physical self-love, which is why seven years seemed to him like a few days.
Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem, so even his service not for its own sake contains something for Hashem's sake.
The word chatas is one of the names of the impure side, while zechus comes from 'zach', pure: the root of all evil is self-interest and the root of all good is acting not for oneself.

marriage as a bond of souls

title.en: Impure klipos versus klipas nogah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the three impure klipos, the forbidden pleasures, cannot be elevated until Moshiach, while klipas nogah, permitted Jewish pleasure, can. He asks how a forbidden thing can then be nullified in sixty, and answers that such nullification is a glimmer of the days of Moshiach.

title.en: The Exodus, the chazir and redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that at the Exodus even the impure klipos were nullified, and brings the Ohr HaChaim on why the pig is called chazir, that it will one day return. He explains that redemption cannot be taken on one's own but comes from Hashem's remembering, and contrasts the Jewish animal soul from nogah with the gentile soul from the impure klipos, which can do nothing for Hashem.

title.en: The Tanya: the nations do good for themselves

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that even the Jewish animal soul is from nogah while the nations' souls are from the three impure klipos with no good at all, so all the good they do is for themselves. Even their mercy is the animal trait shared by all creatures, and they give charity so that they can enjoy their own supper.

title.en: Mercy that becomes a mitzvah; 'the kindness of nations is a sin'

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a man who took in a hungry poor man, gave him everything out of pity, and then added a large sum for the mitzvah of tzedakah. He explains that a Jew's mercy, from nogah, can become a mitzvah, while the nations' kindness is called a sin because they do it to boast that they are good.

title.en: Why Yaakov wept when he kissed Rachel

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yaakov wept when he kissed Rachel, brings the Midrash that people suspected him and Rashi that he saw she would not be buried with him. Through the Gemara that kiddushin is learned from Avraham's purchase of the Machpelah field, he explains that a Jewish marriage is a bond of the soul that continues after death, so the separation in burial pained Yaakov.

title.en: Self-love versus Yaakov's love for Rachel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that physical love is really love of oneself, like loving chicken, which one eats. Yaakov loved Rachel because she was a tzaddekes and part of his soul, and the pain over burial shows it was not physical love. He then asks how seven years could seem like a few days to one who loved so strongly.

title.en: The parable of building a Sukkah

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers with a parable: a Jew who builds his Sukkah in the rain with joy does so because the building itself is for Hashem and part of the mitzvah, so long hours feel like minutes. Yaakov's work for Rachel was like building a Sukkah, a love from holiness, so the years seemed like a few days.

title.en: Hidden love, lishmah and the Maggid of Mezritch

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem, brings a saying of Reb Aharon of Karlin, and says that even a Jew's service not for its own sake holds something for Hashem's sake. He tells how the Maggid of Mezritch, his family starving, sighed, heard that he had lost his world to come, and then learned with great joy now that he could serve purely for Hashem.

title.en: Every Jew is a chassid; the gentile's good

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every Jew at root is a chassid who would do a mitzvah even without reward, and this inner light brings him back. A gentile's good deeds, even when he thinks they are for Heaven, come from the three impure klipos, except for a spark of holiness that can lead to conversion; by contrast, even a Jew's ordinary dealings can be for a mitzvah.

title.en: Chatas and zechus; all will become good

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara on 'the kindness of nations is a sin': their charity adds to their merit and delays the redemption, as with the Emori. He explains that chatas is a name of the impure side, while zechus comes from zach, pure: the root of evil is self-interest and the root of good is acting not for oneself. He closes that in the time of Moshiach even the three impure klipos will become good.

catalogTitle: When Shabbos Ushers in ט' באב

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yirmiyahu was Shlomo HaMelech returned, so that Tisha B'Av is the day of Yirmiyahu and Shemini Atzeres the day of Shlomo, and when Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos, Shlomo comes back as the guest of Shalosh Seudos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Tisha B'Av that falls on Shabbos: the fast is pushed off and one may eat a meal like Shlomo's in his time, yet one stops eating at sunset while shoes may stay on. Since mitzvos work together like the organs of a body, he asks how Shabbos and Tisha B'Av can clash. He tells of Yirmiyahu buying Chanamel's field, and brings the Chasam Sofer: Chanamel hoped a tzaddik's land would be spared, while Yirmiyahu, a reincarnation of Shlomo who overslept on the day the Beis HaMikdash opened, felt he bore the guilt for the Churban. Hashem answered that a new body does not suffer for the old one. Shlomo wrote Shir HaShirim and Yirmiyahu Eichah; Shemini Atzeres is Shlomo's day of perfect union, marked by little eating, nezirus and Shabbos. At Shalosh Seudos of this Shabbos Shlomo returns, and the weeks to Shemini Atzeres turn Yirmiyahu back into Shlomo.

en: When Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos it is pushed off, and the Gemara allows a meal like Shlomo's in his time, yet one stops eating at sunset while shoes may stay on.
The mitzvos are like the organs of a body that work in harmony, so oneg Shabbos and the fast of Tisha B'Av cannot truly contradict each other.
Following the Chasam Sofer, Yirmiyahu was a reincarnation of Shlomo HaMelech and felt responsible for the destruction of the Beis HaMikdash he himself had built.
Tisha B'Av is the day of Yirmiyahu, the prophet of bitterness who wrote Eichah, and Shemini Atzeres is the day of Shlomo, who wrote Shir HaShirim, a day of perfect union.
When Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos, Shlomo HaMelech comes as a guest at Shalosh Seudos, and stopping to eat then is the closeness of that hour, not mourning.
From Tisha B'Av to Shemini Atzeres, Yirmiyahu's face is transformed back into Shlomo's, and the mourning is meant to become the black background of a woven picture of joy.

candidateTopics: Tisha B'Av that falls on Shabbos
Yirmiyahu as a reincarnation of Shlomo HaMelech
Shemini Atzeres as the day of Shlomo

title.en: Tisha B'Av pushed off by Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach says he wants to speak of the lighter side of Tisha B'Av, which this year falls on Shabbos and is pushed off; Rebbi even wished to abolish it then. He asks why one stops eating at sunset while shoes may stay on, and gives the simple answer that eating would spoil the whole fast.

title.en: Mitzvos in harmony like the organs of a body

summary.en: Citing 'mishpetei Hashem emes tzadku yachdav', the Mashgiach compares the 248 mitzvos to the organs of the body, which never contradict each other. He asks how there can then be a clash between oneg Shabbos and the fast of Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Yirmiyahu buys Chanamel's field

summary.en: The Mashgiach retells the prophecy that Yirmiyahu, imprisoned as Yerushalayim was falling, should buy his cousin Chanamel's field as a sign that fields will again be bought and sold, and bury the deeds in an earthen vessel. He then reads Yirmiyahu's prayer, protesting what purpose there is in buying a field that the Kasdim are about to take.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer on Chanamel's intention

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer: Chanamel knew the land would fall to Bavel, but believed punishment has no hold on a tzaddik, so he sold the field to Yirmiyahu while keeping its fruits for his lifetime. Yirmiyahu understood this and felt he was betraying him.

title.en: Yirmiyahu was once Shlomo

summary.en: From the seforim of Kabbalah the Mashgiach relates that Yirmiyahu was a reincarnation of Shlomo HaMelech, who overslept with the Temple keys under his pillow on the morning the Beis HaMikdash was to open. Yirmiyahu therefore felt he, more than anyone, was responsible for the Churban, and that Chanamel's 'insurance policy' was worthless.

title.en: A new body does not suffer for the old

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Yirmiyahu's prayer as a plea to the One who knows how sins pass from gilgul to gilgul: why must he betray his cousin? Hashem answers that He is the G-d of the body as of the soul; a new body that does not repeat the old sins need not suffer for them, a wonderful explanation of the Chasam Sofer.

title.en: Shlomo and Yirmiyahu, two faces of one person

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shlomo and Yirmiyahu are two faces of one person. Shlomo means perfection: his generation knew no war, hunger or poverty, a preview of the days of Moshiach and a perfect union; Yirmiyahu is its opposite, and remembering he was once Shlomo, he wrote Eichah instead of Shir HaShirim.

title.en: Shir HaShirim, Eichah and the Mishnah's 'come out and see'

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Shir HaShirim, a song of union, with Eichah, and explains that Eichah ends 'chadesh yameinu kekedem' as Yirmiyahu's longing to be Shlomo again; the Zera Kodesh distinguishes Yeshayah, prophet of consolation, from Yirmiyahu, prophet of bitterness. He reads the Mishnah at the end of Taanis as saying that on the fifteenth of Av one sees Yirmiyahu turned back into Shlomo.

title.en: Shemini Atzeres, the day of Shlomo

summary.en: The Mashgiach names Shemini Atzeres as the day of Shlomo: its haftarah is Shlomo's dedication of the Beis HaMikdash, the Bnei Yissaschar calls it the day of perfect union, and Shlomo is its guest after David. He asks why the verse describes Shlomo's era as 'each man under his vine and fig tree', and explains that the vine teaches the measure of nezirus and the fig the measure for carrying on Shabbos.

title.en: Nezirus, Shabbos and Shalosh Seudos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that nezirus is the joy of a tzaddik who needs little of this world, and Shabbos is union, the realm of the One as against the realm of the many; in Shlomo's time people lived this way rather than feasting. Shemini Atzeres, with its 'small meal', Koheles and the custom of hardly eating, expresses it, and so does Shalosh Seudos, the highest time of Shabbos.

title.en: Shlomo comes to Shalosh Seudos

summary.en: Returning to his question, the Mashgiach explains that when Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos, the guest at Shalosh Seudos is Shlomo HaMelech, as he was in his time, not as Yirmiyahu. Shabbos Chazon is the highest Shabbos of the year, and as its holiness grows toward sunset one stops eating as at Shemini Atzeres, out of union with Hashem, while shoes stay on because it is not mourning.

title.en: Consolation within the mourning

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Shabbos before Tisha B'Av reads Chazon Yeshayahu, from the prophet of consolation, because Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av. One fasts and weeps, yet the mourning itself is a consolation, as in the story of Napoleon; whoever mourns Yerushalayim merits and sees its joy, especially at Shalosh Seudos of this Shabbos.

title.en: From Tisha B'Av to Shemini Atzeres

summary.en: Bringing the Toras Avos, the Mashgiach explains that the Three Weeks through the Yamim Nora'im are one preparation for Shemini Atzeres: a 'plastic surgery' in which Yirmiyahu's face turns into Shlomo's. The verse 'atah hor'eisa lada'as' from the Tisha B'Av Torah reading is carried along and brought out again at Shemini Atzeres; Yeshayah and Shlomo are both of consolation and building.

title.en: Shlomo conquered the world with peace

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Shlomo as an emperor over the civilized world who, unlike Alexander or Napoleon, conquered with wisdom and peace, as Moshiach ben David will. When he judged the two women he had to send for a sword, since none was in the room; even his police went unarmed.

title.en: Male and female in holiness and impurity

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in holiness the masculine is the stronger and in impurity the feminine, referring to the Ohr HaChaim on Vayechi, and touches on why in the footsteps of Moshiach the feminine forces surface. Hence the land of Sheva was ruled by a queen; citing the Zera Kodesh, he says Sheva is spelled with a beis and denotes the attribute of fire and judgment.

title.en: Building through the mourning

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Queen of Sheva submitted to Shlomo in Yerushalayim, and reads the full spelling of Yerushalayim as Yirmiyahu becoming Shlomo again. Tisha B'Av, he concludes, is a day of sitting on the ground and weeping in order to build: within the full laws of mourning, every person should turn his inner Yirmiyahu into Shlomo, like a colorful bird woven on a black background.

title.en: Hashiveinu: preparing for the consolation

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every person lives through being Shlomo and falling to be Yirmiyahu, and the bitterness of Tisha B'Av is meant to serve his avodas Hashem. He closes with Eichah's last verse, the pain of a gentile rejoicing over the ruins, and a call to rise from the ground and prepare for the consolation and joy of the fifteenth of Av.

catalogTitle: הנשמות חלק אלקי ממעל ממש' 'בנים' אתם לה' אלוקיכם; קשיא: איך יש מדריגות בנשמות אם כלם אלקות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why every Jewish soul is 'truly a part of G-d above' and a child of Hashem drawn from His wisdom, and then takes up the question of how there can be levels among souls, answering with the image of one body from head to heel that runs through the generations down to our own, the heel before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach learns the opening of Tanya chapter two: the second soul of a Jew is truly a part of G-d. From the verse that Hashem breathed into Adam the breath of life, and the saying that one who breathes, breathes from within himself, he shows that this breath carries Hashem's innermost being, which is why the shofar is blown with a cry beyond words. The daily blessing 'You breathed it into me' shows this holds for every Jew. The soul rose in Hashem's thought, and Jews are called His children: as a child is drawn from the father's brain, every soul is drawn from Hashem's wisdom. Since Hashem is Himself the knowledge, as the Rambam writes, the human brain, made for this world, cannot grasp it; the soul and ruach hakodesh can, and the rest is received and believed. He then asks how levels among souls are possible, and explains that one body has a head and a heel, and so do the world and the generations, down to our own heel generation, where truth is lacking.

en: The verse that Hashem 'breathed into his nostrils the breath of life' shows that the soul comes from Hashem's innermost being, since one who breathes breathes from within himself.
The daily blessing 'You breathed it into me' shows that this breath of Hashem is in every Jew, not only in Adam.
Jews are called children of Hashem because, as a child is drawn from the father's brain, every Jewish soul is drawn from Hashem's thought and wisdom.
The human brain was created to understand this world, so it cannot grasp Hashem, who is Himself the knowledge and the knower; this is grasped only by the soul.
The Mashgiach asks how there can be greater and lesser souls if all of them come from Hashem's wisdom, just as all of a man's children are equally his children.
Like the limbs of one body from head to heel, there are levels in the world and in the generations, and our generation is the heel before Moshiach, which hardly feels.
